Whats metal got to do with it? Transition metals in
Clostridioides
 difÞcile infection
Suzanna Y Gomez
1
, Jay Patel
1
and Christopher A Lopez
The enteric pathogen Clostridioides difÞcile overcomes barriers
to
 colonization imposed by the microbiota and host immune
response
 to induce disease. To navigate the dynamic gut
environment,
 C. difÞcile must respond to dietary and host-
mediated
 ßuctuations in transition metal availability. Transition
metals
 are required trace nutrients that foster inter-microbial
competition
 when limited, inhibit bacterial growth through host
sequestration,
 or induce toxicity in excess. This review
highlights
 recent evidence that transition metals inßuence
multiple
 stages of C. difÞcile colonization and that C. difÞcile
initiates
 a coordinated response to maintain metal-dependent
homeostasis.
 Further exploration of the mechanisms of C.
difÞcile
 metal sensing and nutrient competition with the
microbiota
 will be necessary for the therapeutic manipulation of
the
 gut environment during C. difÞcile infection.

Introduction
Nutrients are key drivers in shaping the ecology of
organisms
 within an environment [1]. In the mammalian
gastrointestinal
 tract, nutrient availability is one factor
controlling
 the diversity of the commensal bacteria, which
in
 turn inßuences host immune responses, metabolism,
and
 other critical processes [2,3]. Transition metals that
include
 iron (Fe), zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), and nickel
(Ni)
 are trace elements necessary for all bacteria by
serving
 as structural components in proteins and as enzy-
matic
 cofactors [4]. Limited metal availability initiates
stress
 responses that reprogram metabolic pathways,
increase
 production of proteins involved in metal uptake,
and
 alter virulence factor expression [5]. Yet, maintaining
intracellular
 metal pools must be balanced with avoidingtoxic
 high metal concentrations. The coordinated control
of
 metal availability is referred to as metallostasis [5].
Clostridioides
 difÞcile is a spore-forming bacterium that
typically
 colonizes the intestines following dysbiosis, or
disruption
 of the commensal microbiota [6]. Spores enter-
ing
 the intestines subsequent to dysbiosis germinate into
vegetative
 C. difÞcile, which produce toxins that trigger a
robust
 inßammatory response that further destabilizes the
resident
 microbiota [7]. Throughout the cycle of C. difÞcile
colonization,
 infection, and transmission, metal availabil-
ity
 is controlled through the actions of the microbiota that
may
 compete for those metals and by the immune
response
 that limits metal concentrations in a process
termed
 nutritional immunity. Here, we provide a brief
overview
 of recent advancements in understanding the
factors
 that control metal availability during C. difÞcile
infection
 (CDI) and how C. difÞcile responds to those
shifting
 metal concentrations to successfully colonize the
intestines.
Transition metal availability and the
microbiota
Approximately 90% of the gut bacteria in adult humans
are
 from the phyla Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, with
Actinobacteria,
 Verrucumicrobia, and Proteobacteria col-
lectively
 making up less than 10% of the remaining
microbiota
 [8]. This diverse microbiota protects against
overgrowth
 of pathogenic bacteria through a process
called
 colonization resistance [9]. Disruption of coloniza-
tion
 resistance is a primary risk factor that increases
susceptibility
 to CDI and can be caused by antibiotic
use
 or underlying inßammatory disorders [10

,11

]. Large
ßuctuations
 in nutrient metal availability, either through
supplementation
 or deÞciency, can similarly alter the
microbiota
 composition to decrease colonization resis-
tance
 (Figure 1) [12,13].
Nearly
 all bacteria require Fe, thus changes in dietary Fe
availability
 can impact the abundances of bacteria in the
intestines
 [13,14]. Limited Fe can force competition,
allowing
 bacteria such as members of the Enterobacter-
iaceae
 to outcompete other bacteria through multiple
mechanisms
 including the production of high Fe-afÞnity
siderophores
 that capture ferric iron (Fe
3+
) [12,15,16].
Consistent
 with this notion, an increase in the proportion
of
 Escherichia coli was observed in mice fed low Fe diets
and
 was associated with increased transcription of side-
rophore
 import genes [17]. Alternatively, Fe supplemen-
tation
 in conjunction with inßammation also leads to

changes in the microbiota characterized by an increase in
Proteobacteria
 [18] and a decrease in beneÞcial butyrate-
producing
 Clostridia including Faecalibacterium prausnit-
zii
 and Ruminococcus bromii [19]. While there is variation in
the
 speciÞc populations affected by Fe deÞciency and
supplementation,
 multiple studies support Enterobacter-
iaceae
 blooms as a biomarker of microbiota destabiliza-
tion
 [20]. Indeed, in a mouse CDI model, Enterobacter-
iaceae
 blooms following low-dose antibiotic treatments
predicts
 susceptibility to C. difÞcile colonization [21

]. In
humans,
 adults symptomatically and asymptomatically
colonized
 with C. difÞcile have higher abundances of
Enterobacteriaceae
 compared to non-colonized individu-
als
 [22]. A similar trend is observed in elderly patients
with
 CDI, where C. difÞcile is associated with increased E.
coli
 and decreased F. prausnitzii abundances [23]. Despite
similar
 patterns of dysbiosis between microbiota
experiencing
 changes in Fe availability and microbiota
during
 CDI, there is limited evidence that directly links
dietary
 Fe to CDI susceptibility. A possible explanation
could
 be that changes in Fe availability only affect CDI
susceptibility
 in conjunction with other CDI risk factors.
In
 accordance with this idea, supplementation of another
dietary
 metal, Zn, only allowed C. difÞcile to colonizewhen
 combined with antibiotics. In this study, excess
dietary
 Zn increased the proportion of Enterococcus and
Clostridia
 XI while decreasing Turicibacter populations
[24].
 The excess Zn-induced dysbiosis then lowered
the
 dose of antibiotics necessary to reduce colonization
resistance
 against C. difÞcile [24,25]. Overall, as necessary
nutrients,
 extreme changes in Fe and Zn concentrations
can
 drastically inßuence the microbiota and synergize
with
 other risk factors to alter susceptibility to CDI.
Inammation and nutritional immunity: a
changing
 landscape
During CDI, toxin-mediated intestinal inßammation
induces
 host immune responses that change metal avail-
ability
 (Figure 2). C. difÞcile produces two primary toxins,
TcdA
 and TcdB, involved in intestinal inßammation and
epithelial
 damage [26]. The host immune response to
these
 toxins is in part characterized by an inßux of
neutrophils
 that release cytosolic calprotectin (CP) [7].
CP
 is a heterodimeric protein of S100A8 and S100A9 that
sequesters
 divalent Þrst row transition metals at two sites
at
 the dimer interface [27] to limit bioavailable Zn, Fe, Ni,
Mn,
 and copper (Cu) [28

,29Ð32]. Neutrophils and epi-
thelial
 cells also release lipocalin-2, or neutrophil gelati-
nase-associated
 lipocalin (NGAL), during inßammation
[33].
 Lipocalin-2 interferes with bacterial Fe uptake by
binding
 to catecholate siderophores [33]. Fecal CP and
lipocalin-2
 concentrations are clinically used as biomark-
ers
 of inßammation severity [34,35] and shape the gut
environment
 by altering metal availability.
While
 CP and lipocalin-2 limit metal acquisition, toxin-
mediated
 epithelial damage and edema cause intestinal
hemorrhaging
 and the release of Fe-containing heme
through
 hemoglobin degradation [36Ð38]. Excessive
heme
 accumulation is toxic to C. difÞcile [36], requiring
the
 bacterium to adapt to high levels of luminal heme for
survival.
Changes
 in metal oxidation states also likely occur during
CDI.
 Antibiotic treatment and CDI in murine models
increase
 tissue oxygenation in colonic epithelial cells
[39,40].
 Oxygen diffusing into the lumen can then oxidize
soluble
 ferrous Fe (Fe
2+
) to form less soluble Fe
3+
(Fig-
ure
 2). Changes in metal accessibility due to oxidation,
along
 with sequestration by host immune proteins and the
risk
 of heme toxicity during CDI, contribute to a dynamic
intestinal
 environment in which C. difÞcile must adapt to
continue
 thriving.
Adaptation to nutrient metal availability
Iron regulation
Fe is limited in the inßamed intestines due to chelation
by
 host Fe-binding proteins [41] and environmental
conditions
 that oxidize Fe
2+
to Fe
3+
, as discussed in
the
 previous section (Figure 2). In C. difÞcile, the relative
abundance
 of Fe is detected primarily by the ferric-

conditions
 and binds DNA [42]. As in other bacteria [42],
Fur
 typically represses gene transcription when bound to
Fe
 [43]. Fur de-repression in an Fe-deplete environment
results
 in the transcription of multiple genes with roles in
metallostasis
 and metabolism [44]. Amongst the genes
involved
 in metallostasis are zupT (zinc transporter), a
putative
 fhu operon (predicted siderophore uptake), and
feo
 genes (ferrous iron importers) (Figure 3) [44]. ZupT is
highly
 expressed under Fe-limited and Zn-limited con-
ditions
 [43,45Ð47] and imports Zn in response to CP [45].
The
 expression of a Zn-importer under Fe-starvation may
be
 due to CP-mediated chelation of both metals under
physiological
 conditions [28

]. Thus, during infection the
presence
 of CP may indicate both Zn and Fe limitation,
prompting
 C. difÞcile to respond to reduced availability of
these
 metals. Alternatively, C. difÞcile may have evolved
cross-regulation
 of Fe and Zn starvation responses similar
to
 those described in Staphylococcus aureus where both Fur
and
 a Zn-uptake regulator (Zur) coordinate transcription
of
 the metallophore staphylopine [48]. Though no func-
tional
 Zur is described in C. difÞcile, other regulatorymechanisms
 may mediate cross-regulation with multiple
stress
 responses. This type of non-Fur family regulation
was
 observed in Clostridium beijernckii, where Fe
2+
bound
to
 AdhR de-repressed metabolic adhA1 and adhA2 expres-
sion
 [49

].
Genes
 in the fhu operon are homologous to genes encod-
ing
 siderophore uptake machinery [50]. However, no
siderophore
 biosynthesis pathways are described for C.
difÞcile,
 leaving the intriguing possibility that C. difÞcile
may
 engage in siderophore piracy and transport micro-
biota-produced
 siderophores similar to Bacteroides thetaio-
taomicron
 [51

]. Ferrous Fe transporters encoded by feoB
and
 feoA are widespread amongst Bacteria [52]. FeoB is an
integrated
 membrane protein with a G-protein domain
and
 provides the route of entry for Fe
2+
[52]. The func-
tion
 of cytosolic FeoA is unknown, though recent reports
propose
 a model where FeoA interacts with FeoB to
modulate
 GTPase activity and Fe import [53]. While
most
 bacteria encode a single feoAB operon [52], C. difÞcile
encodes
 multiple feoAB systems [40]. For instance, the
common
 laboratory strain 630 encodes 3 feoB and 5 feoA

Fe
2+
import via FeoAB can inﬂuence not only metallos-
tasis,
 but can alter clinically relevant aspects of C. difﬁcile
physiology.
 Mutation of feoB1 induces an Fe starvation
response
 that shifts C. difﬁcile metabolism towards path-
ways
 that decrease sensitivity to the antibiotic metroni-
dazole
 [54

], which served as a frontline antibiotic in the
treatment
 of CDI [55]. The factors that regulate the
production
 of C. difﬁcile feoA and feoB and how multiple
copies
 of these genes enable C. difﬁcile to survive in the
intestines
 warrant further investigation.
Fe
 limitation also alters transcription of metabolic genes
(for
 a full view, see Ref. [44]). For example, proline
reduction
 via a proline reductase supports energy produc-
tion
 and the maintenance of redox balance. Increased
availability
 of proline or hydroxyproline, a component of
collagen,
 opens a niche from which C. difﬁcile can compete
with
 the microbiota [46,56

]. Under Fe-limitedconditions,
 C. difﬁcile increases transcription of proline
reductase
 genes, shifting energy production from glycol-
ysis
 to amino acid fermentation via Stickland reactions
[44].
 Decreased ﬂux through central carbon catabolic
pathways,
 largely owing to reliance of those pathways
on
 Fe-containing ferredoxins and Fe-sulfur clusters, is a
key
 metabolic signature for C. difﬁcile in a Fe-deplete
environment.
Heme stress
The inﬂux of heme during CDI could potentiate detri-
mental
 reactive oxygen species generation [41]. To limit
the
 toxic effects of heme overabundance, C. difﬁcile
encodes
 two systems that are speciﬁcally responsive to
heme.
 Heme binding to the transcriptional regulator
HatR
 will de-repress transcription of hatT, an efﬂux pump
that
 limits intracellular heme concentrations [36]. Under
high
 heme stress, the regulator HsmR activates transcrip-
tion
 of HsmA to incorporate heme into the cytoplasmic

Zinc regulation
In response to CP-mediated Zn sequestration, C. difÞcile
upregulates
 transcription of many of the same genes that
increase
 under Fe limitation [44,46], similar to that
observed
 in Acinetobacter baumannii where CP elicited a
dual
 Zn/Fe response [28

]. As part of the response to CP,
C.
 difÞcile upregulates zupT, which enables C. difÞcile to
overcome
 CP Zn sequestration in a mouse model of CDI
[45].
 The selenoprotein proline reductase is also more
highly
 transcribed in C. difÞcile grown with CP [46].
Furthermore,
 deletion of selenoprotein synthesis inhibits
function
 of the proline reductase with concomitant
increases
 in the expression of genes involved in mannitol
catabolism,
 possibly shifting C. difÞcile metabolism away
from
 Stickland fermentation and towards mannitol fer-
mentation
 [59]. Combined, these studies suggest an
interplay
 between Zn and selenoprotein synthesis that
inßuence
 metabolic pathways relevant to C. difÞcile
colonization.
Other nutrient metals
Aside from Fe and Zn, there is limited data on the roles
other
 nutrient metals play in C. difÞcile physiology and
virulence.
 C. difÞcile encodes two Mn-dependent catalases
(cotD,
 cotG) and a Mn-dependent superoxide dismutase
(sodA)
 that are associated with the spore coat [60]. As
these
 genes are not upregulated in the presence of oxygen
[40,61],
 it is likely they perform a function associated with
spore
 maturation or protection rather than ROS detoxiÞ-
cation
 in vegetative C. difÞcile. Mn is also required for
Þbronectin-binding
 in Fbp68, which may enable C. difÞ-
cile
 attachment to host cell surfaces during infection [62].
Recently,
 a putative Ni-uptake system was identiÞed
through
 comparison of a peptide transporter in C. difÞcile,
OppA,
 with the Ni-binding protein NikZ in Campylobacter
jejuni
 [63]. This led to the hypothesis that OppA functions
as
 a Ni-transporter for Ni-dependent enzymes like urease
[63].
 However, the full contribution of Mn and Ni avail-
ability
 on CDI remain an open area of exploration.
Conclusion
From the initial changes to the microbiota that increase
colonization
 susceptibility to the subsequent immune
response,
 changes in nutrient metal accessibility inßu-
ence
 C. difÞcile colonization and survival. While there are
many
 unknown details in how C. difÞcile controls its
responses
 to environmental ßuctuations in metal concen-
trations,
 there are two areas in particular that may be
fruitful
 topics for future exploration. First, how does C.difÞcile
 sense and respond to limitation of non-Fe metals
like
 Zn and Mn and what are the effects on C. difÞcile
colonization?
 Second, how does metal availability impact
C.
 difÞcile interactions with the microbiota? Illuminating
these
 avenues of the host-microbe-C. difÞcile interplay
will
 ultimately broaden our understanding of the adapta-
tion
 strategies inherent in this pathogen.

Nutrients are key drivers in shaping the ecology of
organisms

in

and

include

serving

matic

increase

and

intracellular

Clostridioides

typically

disruption

vegetative

robust

resident

colonization,

ity

may

response
 that limits metal concentrations in a process
termed

overview
 of recent advancements in understanding the
factors

infection
 (CDI) and how C. difÞcile responds to those
shifting

intestines.

microbiota

are

Actinobacteria,

lectively

microbiota
 [8]. This diverse microbiota protects against
overgrowth
 of pathogenic bacteria through a process
called

tion

susceptibility
 to CDI and can be caused by antibiotic
use


,11

]. Large
ßuctuations

supplementation

microbiota

tance

Nearly

availability

allowing

mechanisms

siderophores

of

and

In response to CP-mediated Zn sequestration, C. difÞcile

Furthermore,

increases

inßuence

Other nutrient metals
Aside from Fe and Zn, there is limited data on the roles
other
 nutrient metals play in C. difÞcile physiology and
virulence.
 C. difÞcile encodes two Mn-dependent catalases
(cotD,
 cotG) and a Mn-dependent superoxide dismutase
(sodA)
 that are associated with the spore coat [60]. As
these
 genes are not upregulated in the presence of oxygen
[40,61],
 it is likely they perform a function associated with
spore
 maturation or protection rather than ROS detoxiÞ-
cation
 in vegetative C. difÞcile. Mn is also required for
Þbronectin-binding
 in Fbp68, which may enable C. difÞ-
cile
 attachment to host cell surfaces during infection [62].
Recently,
 a putative Ni-uptake system was identiÞed
through
 comparison of a peptide transporter in C. difÞcile,
OppA,
 with the Ni-binding protein NikZ in Campylobacter
jejuni
 [63]. This led to the hypothesis that OppA functions
as
 a Ni-transporter for Ni-dependent enzymes like urease
[63].
 However, the full contribution of Mn and Ni avail-
ability
 on CDI remain an open area of exploration.
Conclusion
From the initial changes to the microbiota that increase
colonization
 susceptibility to the subsequent immune
response,
 changes in nutrient metal accessibility inßu-
ence
 C. difÞcile colonization and survival. While there are
many
 unknown details in how C. difÞcile controls its
responses
 to environmental ßuctuations in metal concen-
trations,
 there are two areas in particular that may be
fruitful
 topics for future exploration. First, how does C.difÞcile
 sense and respond to limitation of non-Fe metals
like
 Zn and Mn and what are the effects on C. difÞcile
colonization?
 Second, how does metal availability impact
C.
 difÞcile interactions with the microbiota? Illuminating
these
 avenues of the host-microbe-C. difÞcile interplay
will
 ultimately broaden our understanding of the adapta-
tion
 strategies inherent in this pathogen.

Nutrients are key drivers in shaping the ecology of

include

(Ni)

serving

matic

and

Clostridioides

shifting

intestines.


]. As part of the response to CP,
C.

overcome

[45].

Furthermore,

from

Other nutrient metals
Aside from Fe and Zn, there is limited data on the roles
other
 nutrient metals play in C. difÞcile physiology and
virulence.
 C. difÞcile encodes two Mn-dependent catalases
(cotD,

(sodA)

these

[40,61],
 it is likely they perform a function associated with
spore

cation

Þbronectin-binding

Recently,
 a putative Ni-uptake system was identiÞed
through

OppA,

jejuni
 [63]. This led to the hypothesis that OppA functions
as

[63].
 However, the full contribution of Mn and Ni avail-
ability
 on CDI remain an open area of exploration.
Conclusion
From the initial changes to the microbiota that increase
colonization
 susceptibility to the subsequent immune
response,
 changes in nutrient metal accessibility inßu-
ence
 C. difÞcile colonization and survival. While there are
many
 unknown details in how C. difÞcile controls its
responses
 to environmental ßuctuations in metal concen-
trations,
 there are two areas in particular that may be
fruitful
 topics for future exploration. First, how does C.difÞcile
 sense and respond to limitation of non-Fe metals
like
 Zn and Mn and what are the effects on C. difÞcile
colonization?
 Second, how does metal availability impact
C.
 difÞcile interactions with the microbiota? Illuminating
these
 avenues of the host-microbe-C. difÞcile interplay
will

tion

## AbstractThe enteric pathogen *Clostridioides difficile* overcomes barriers to colonization imposed by the microbiota and host immune response to induce disease. To navigate the dynamic gut environment, *C. difficile* must respond to dietary and host-mediated fluctuations in transition metal availability. Transition metals are required trace nutrients that foster inter-microbial competition when limited, inhibit bacterial growth through host sequestration, or induce toxicity in excess. This review highlights recent evidence that transition metals influence multiple stages of *C. difficile* colonization and that *C. difficile* initiates a coordinated response to maintain metal-dependent homeostasis. Further exploration of the mechanisms of *C. difficile* metal sensing and nutrient competition with the microbiota will be necessary for the therapeutic manipulation of the gut environment during *C. difficile* infection.

## IntroductionNutrients are key drivers in shaping the ecology of organisms within an environment [1]. In the mammalian gastrointestinal tract, nutrient availability is one factor controlling the diversity of the commensal bacteria, which in turn influences host immune responses, metabolism, and other critical processes [2,3]. Transition metals that include iron (Fe), zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), and nickel (Ni) are trace elements necessary for all bacteria by serving as structural components in proteins and as enzymatic cofactors [4]. Limited metal availability initiates stress responses that reprogram metabolic pathways, increase production of proteins involved in metal uptake, and alter virulence factor expression [5]. Yet, maintaining intracellular metal pools must be balanced with avoiding toxic high metal concentrations. The coordinated control of metal availability is referred to as metallostasis [5].

*Clostridioides difficile* is a spore-forming bacterium that typically colonizes the intestines following dysbiosis, or disruption of the commensal microbiota [6]. Spores entering the intestines subsequent to dysbiosis germinate into vegetative *C. difficile*, which produce toxins that trigger a robust inflammatory response that further destabilizes the resident microbiota [7]. Throughout the cycle of *C. difficile* colonization, infection, and transmission, metal availability is controlled through the actions of the microbiota that may compete for those metals and by the immune response that limits metal concentrations in a process termed nutritional immunity. Here, we provide a brief overview of recent advancements in understanding the factors that control metal availability during *C. difficile* infection (CDI) and how *C. difficile* responds to those shifting metal concentrations to successfully colonize the intestines.

## Transition metal availability and the microbiotaApproximately90% of the gut bacteria in adult humans are from the phyla Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, with Actinobacteria, Verrucumicrobia, and Proteobacteria collectively making up less than10% of the remaining microbiota [8]. This diverse microbiota protects against overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria through a process called colonization resistance [9]. Disruption of colonization resistance is a primary risk factor that increases susceptibility to CDI and can be caused by antibiotic use or underlying inflammatory disorders [10,11]. Large fluctuations in nutrient metal availability, either through supplementation or deficiency, can similarly alter the microbiota composition to decrease colonization resistance (Figure1) [12,13].

Nearly all bacteria require Fe, thus changes in dietary Fe availability can impact the abundances of bacteria in the intestines [13,14]. Limited Fe can force competition, allowing bacteria such as members of the Enterobacteriaceae to outcompete other bacteria through multiple mechanisms including the production of high Fe-affinity siderophores that capture ferric iron (Fe³⁺) [12,15,16]. Consistent with this notion, an increase in the proportion of *Escherichia coli* was observed in mice fed low Fe diets and was associated with increased transcription of siderophore import genes [17]. Alternatively, Fe supplementation in conjunction with inflammation also leads to changes in the microbiota characterized by an increase in Proteobacteria [18] and a decrease in beneficial butyrate-producing Clostridia including *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Ruminococcus bromii* [19]. While there is variation in the specific populations affected by Fe deficiency and supplementation, multiple studies support Enterobacteriaceae blooms as a biomarker of microbiota destabilization [20]. Indeed, in a mouse CDI model, Enterobacteriaceae blooms following low-dose antibiotic treatments predicts susceptibility to *C. difficile* colonization [21]. In humans, adults symptomatically and asymptomatically colonized with *C. difficile* have higher abundances of Enterobacteriaceae compared to non-colonized individuals [22]. A similar trend is observed in elderly patients with CDI, where *C. difficile* is associated with increased *E. coli* and decreased *F. prausnitzii* abundances [23]. Despite similar patterns of dysbiosis between microbiota experiencing changes in Fe availability and microbiota during CDI, there is limited evidence that directly links dietary Fe to CDI susceptibility. A possible explanation could be that changes in Fe availability only affect CDI susceptibility in conjunction with other CDI risk factors. In accordance with this idea, supplementation of another dietary metal, Zn, only allowed *C. difficile* to colonize when combined with antibiotics. In this study, excess dietary Zn increased the proportion of *Enterococcus* and Clostridia XI while decreasing *Turicibacter* populations [24]. The excess Zn-induced dysbiosis then lowered the dose of antibiotics necessary to reduce colonization resistance against *C. difficile* [24,25]. Overall, as necessary nutrients, extreme changes in Fe and Zn concentrations can drastically influence the microbiota and synergize with other risk factors to alter susceptibility to CDI.

**Figure1.** Association of iron and zinc with susceptibility towards *Clostridioides difficile* infection. Under homeostatic conditions, commensal microbes in the gut provide colonization resistance against pathogenic bacteria. Limited iron availability can destabilize the microbiota, increasing the relative abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. Iron excess and inflammation similarly alter the microbiota through promoting a bloom of Enterobacteriaceae while decreasing abundance of beneficial Clostridia. Excess zinc synergizes with antibiotic use to lower the antibiotic threshold for *C. difficile* colonization through changes in the microbiota, increasing the risk of infection. CDI — *Clostridioides difficile* infection.

## Inflammation and nutritional immunity: a changing landscapeDuring CDI, toxin-mediated intestinal inflammation induces host immune responses that change metal availability (Figure2). *C. difficile* produces two primary toxins, TcdA and TcdB, involved in intestinal inflammation and epithelial damage [26]. The host immune response to these toxins is in part characterized by an influx of neutrophils that release cytosolic calprotectin (CP) [7]. CP is a heterodimeric protein of S100A8 and S100A9 that sequesters divalent first row transition metals at two sites at the dimer interface [27] to limit bioavailable Zn, Fe, Ni, Mn, and copper (Cu) [28,29–32]. Neutrophils and epithelial cells also release lipocalin-2, or neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), during inflammation [33]. Lipocalin-2 interferes with bacterial Fe uptake by binding to catecholate siderophores [33]. Fecal CP and lipocalin-2 concentrations are clinically used as biomarkers of inflammation severity [34,35] and shape the gut environment by altering metal availability.

While CP and lipocalin-2 limit metal acquisition, toxin-mediated epithelial damage and edema cause intestinal hemorrhaging and the release of Fe-containing heme through hemoglobin degradation [36–38]. Excessive heme accumulation is toxic to *C. difficile* [36], requiring the bacterium to adapt to high levels of luminal heme for survival.

Changes in metal oxidation states also likely occur during CDI. Antibiotic treatment and CDI in murine models increase tissue oxygenation in colonic epithelial cells [39,40]. Oxygen diffusing into the lumen can then oxidize soluble ferrous Fe (Fe²⁺) to form less soluble Fe³⁺ (Figure2). Changes in metal accessibility due to oxidation, along with sequestration by host immune proteins and the risk of heme toxicity during CDI, contribute to a dynamic intestinal environment in which *C. difficile* must adapt to continue thriving.

## Adaptation to nutrient metal availability### Iron regulationFe is limited in the inflamed intestines due to chelation by host Fe-binding proteins [41] and environmental conditions that oxidize Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, as discussed in the previous section (Figure2). In *C. difficile*, the relative abundance of Fe is detected primarily by the ferric uptake regulator (Fur), which dimerizes under Fe-replete conditions and binds DNA [42]. As in other bacteria [42], Fur typically represses gene transcription when bound to Fe [43]. Fur de-repression in an Fe-deplete environment results in the transcription of multiple genes with roles in metallostasis and metabolism [44]. Amongst the genes involved in metallostasis are *zupT* (zinc transporter), a putative *fhu* operon (predicted siderophore uptake), and *feo* genes (ferrous iron importers) (Figure3) [44]. ZupT is highly expressed under Fe-limited and Zn-limited conditions [43,45–47] and imports Zn in response to CP [45]. The expression of a Zn-importer under Fe-starvation may be due to CP-mediated chelation of both metals under physiological conditions [28]. Thus, during infection the presence of CP may indicate both Zn and Fe limitation, prompting *C. difficile* to respond to reduced availability of these metals. Alternatively, *C. difficile* may have evolved cross-regulation of Fe and Zn starvation responses similar to those described in *Staphylococcus aureus* where both Fur and a Zn-uptake regulator (Zur) coordinate transcription of the metallophore staphylopine [48]. Though no functional Zur is described in *C. difficile*, other regulatory mechanisms may mediate cross-regulation with multiple stress responses. This type of non-Fur family regulation was observed in *Clostridium beijerinckii*, where Fe²⁺ bound to AdhR de-repressed metabolic *adhA1* and *adhA2* expression [49].

Genes in the *fhu* operon are homologous to genes encoding siderophore uptake machinery [50]. However, no siderophore biosynthesis pathways are described for *C. difficile*, leaving the intriguing possibility that *C. difficile* may engage in siderophore piracy and transport microbiota-produced siderophores similar to *Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron* [51]. Ferrous Fe transporters encoded by *feoB* and *feoA* are widespread amongst Bacteria [52]. FeoB is an integrated membrane protein with a G-protein domain and provides the route of entry for Fe²⁺ [52]. The function of cytosolic FeoA is unknown, though recent reports propose a model where FeoA interacts with FeoB to modulate GTPase activity and Fe import [53]. While most bacteria encode a single *feoAB* operon [52], *C. difficile* encodes multiple *feoAB* systems [40]. For instance, the common laboratory strain630 encodes3 *feoB* and5 *feoA* genes, with only some of these regulated by Fur [43,44]. Fe²⁺ import via FeoAB can influence not only metallostasis, but can alter clinically relevant aspects of *C. difficile* physiology. Mutation of *feoB1* induces an Fe starvation response that shifts *C. difficile* metabolism towards pathways that decrease sensitivity to the antibiotic metronidazole [54], which served as a frontline antibiotic in the treatment of CDI [55]. The factors that regulate the production of *C. difficile* *feoA* and *feoB* and how multiple copies of these genes enable *C. difficile* to survive in the intestines warrant further investigation.

Fe limitation also alters transcription of metabolic genes (for a full view, see Ref. [44]). For example, proline reduction via a proline reductase supports energy production and the maintenance of redox balance. Increased availability of proline or hydroxyproline, a component of collagen, opens a niche from which *C. difficile* can compete with the microbiota [46,56]. Under Fe-limited conditions, *C. difficile* increases transcription of proline reductase genes, shifting energy production from glycolysis to amino acid fermentation via Stickland reactions [44]. Decreased flux through central carbon catabolic pathways, largely owing to reliance of those pathways on Fe-containing ferredoxins and Fe-sulfur clusters, is a key metabolic signature for *C. difficile* in a Fe-deplete environment.

### Heme stressThe influx of heme during CDI could potentiate detrimental reactive oxygen species generation [41]. To limit the toxic effects of heme overabundance, *C. difficile* encodes two systems that are specifically responsive to heme. Heme binding to the transcriptional regulator HatR will de-repress transcription of *hatT*, an efflux pump that limits intracellular heme concentrations [36]. Under high heme stress, the regulator HsmR activates transcription of *HsmA* to incorporate heme into the cytoplasmic membrane [57]. Heme-bound HsmA decreases sensitivity to oxidative stress and to the antibiotic vancomycin [57], a current first-line treatment for primary CDI [55]. Additionally, mutations in *hsmA* can confer resistance to metronidazole [58]. Combined, the HatRT and HsmRA systems protect *C. difficile* from toxic concentrations of heme released during inflammation.

### Zinc regulationIn response to CP-mediated Zn sequestration, *C. difficile* upregulates transcription of many of the same genes that increase under Fe limitation [44,46], similar to that observed in *Acinetobacter baumannii* where CP elicited a dual Zn/Fe response [28]. As part of the response to CP, *C. difficile* upregulates *zupT*, which enables *C. difficile* to overcome CP Zn sequestration in a mouse model of CDI [45]. The selenoprotein proline reductase is also more highly transcribed in *C. difficile* grown with CP [46]. Furthermore, deletion of selenoprotein synthesis inhibits function of the proline reductase with concomitant increases in the expression of genes involved in mannitol catabolism, possibly shifting *C. difficile* metabolism away from Stickland fermentation and towards mannitol fermentation [59]. Combined, these studies suggest an interplay between Zn and selenoprotein synthesis that influence metabolic pathways relevant to *C. difficile* colonization.

### Other nutrient metalsAside from Fe and Zn, there is limited data on the roles other nutrient metals play in *C. difficile* physiology and virulence. *C. difficile* encodes two Mn-dependent catalases (*cotD*, *cotG*) and a Mn-dependent superoxide dismutase (*sodA*) that are associated with the spore coat [60]. As these genes are not upregulated in the presence of oxygen [40,61], it is likely they perform a function associated with spore maturation or protection rather than ROS detoxification in vegetative *C. difficile*. Mn is also required for fibronectin-binding in Fbp68, which may enable *C. difficile* attachment to host cell surfaces during infection [62]. Recently, a putative Ni-uptake system was identified through comparison of a peptide transporter in *C. difficile*, OppA, with the Ni-binding protein NikZ in *Campylobacter jejuni* [63]. This led to the hypothesis that OppA functions as a Ni-transporter for Ni-dependent enzymes like urease [63]. However, the full contribution of Mn and Ni availability on CDI remain an open area of exploration.

## ConclusionFrom the initial changes to the microbiota that increase colonization susceptibility to the subsequent immune response, changes in nutrient metal accessibility influence *C. difficile* colonization and survival. While there are many unknown details in how *C. difficile* controls its responses to environmental fluctuations in metal concentrations, there are two areas in particular that may be fruitful topics for future exploration. First, how does *C. difficile* sense and respond to limitation of non-Fe metals like Zn and Mn and what are the effects on *C. difficile* colonization? Second, how does metal availability impact *C. difficile* interactions with the microbiota? Illuminating these avenues of the host-microbe-*C. difficile* interplay will ultimately broaden our understanding of the adaptation strategies inherent in this pathogen.

AbstractClostridioides difÞcileis one of the most common nosocomial gastrointestinal
pathogens, and recurrence is a problematic issue because approximately 20e30% of patients
experience at least one episode of recurrence, even after treatment with a therapeutic drug
of choice forC. difÞcileinfection (CDI), such as vancomycin. CDI recurrence has a multifacto-
rial complex mechanism, in which gut microbiota disruption coincident with viableC. difÞcile
spores, is considered the most important factor. The effectiveness of an anti-C. difÞcileanti-
microbial agent against CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect onC. difÞcilespores and
vice versa. However, an antimicrobial agent, such as Þdaxomicin, which has a good inhibitory
effect on bothC. difÞcilevegetative cells and spores is assumed to not only treat CDI but also
prevent its recurrence. Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been proposed as a
possible mechanism of inhibiting spores, and as a result, redesigning anti-C. difÞcileantimicro-
bial agents with the ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another pathway for the
development of anti-C. difÞcilespore agents. For example, vancomycin lacks an inhibitory ef-
fect againstC. difÞcilespores, but a vancomycin-loaded spore-targeting iron oxide nanopar-
ticle that selectively binds toC. difÞcilespores has been developed to successfully delay
spore germination. Some new antimicrobial agents in phase II clinical trials, including cadazo-
lid and ridinilazole, have shown exceptional anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects that
can be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence in the future.

Introduction
Clostridioides difﬁcileis one of the most common nosoco-
mial gastrointestinal pathogens, with clinical presentations
ranging from mild diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis
to toxic megacolon, with a mortality of up to 25e40%.
1e9
Severe colitis develops in approximately 3% of patients
withC. difﬁcileinfection (CDI) who may have paradoxical
decrease in the amount of diarrhea after ileus or toxic
megacolon developed.
3,10
Diagnosis of CDI relies on the
detection of toxigenicC. difﬁcile, its toxins or toxin genes
in stool.
9,11
Metronidazole was suggested for mild CDI and vanco-
mycin was recommended for severe CDI.
8
Nevertheless,
oral vancomycin and ﬁdaxomicin have been suggested to
replace metronidazole as the therapeutic choice for either
mild-moderate or severe CDI in the Clinical Practice
Guidelines forC. difﬁcileInfection in Adults and Children:
2017 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America
(IDSA) and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America
(SHEA).
12
For patients with severe and fulminant forms of
CDI presenting as ileus, oral intake of vancomycin or
ﬁdaxomicin is disrupted because of the obstruction of the
gut because ﬁdaxomicin can only be administered orally;
and vancomycin, either administered orally or intra-
rectally. This leads to marked disruption of the microbiota,
leading to prolonged loss of colonization resistance toC.
difﬁcileand dense colonization by vancomycin-resistant
Enterococcus,K. pneumoniae, andE. coli.
13
Although antimicrobial resistance is not clinically prob-
lematic, treating CDI with metronidazole and vancomycin is
associated with a high treatment failure rate and high
relapse rate.
14
According to the Clinical Practice Guidelines
by IDSA/SHEA, oral vancomycin was still the drug of choice
for recurrentC. difﬁcileassociated diarrhea, but the rate
of second recurrence rate is as high as 22.6e41.8%, despite
successful treatment with vancomycin.
15
The high recur-
rence rate of CDI after treatment might be due to the
generation of spores that lead to persistence of CDI.
16,17
The biology of spores in the pathogenesis ofC.
difﬁcile
Owing to its strict anaerobic requirements, the infectious
and transmissible morphotype ofC. difﬁcileis a dormant
spore, which is characterized by resistance to heat, oxy-
gen, and common disinfectants, such as ethanol-based
hand sanitizers.
16,18,19
The sporeeresistance properties
are attributed to a low water content (25e60% of wet
weight), elevated levels of dipicolonic acid (25% of core dry
weight) chelated with calcium, and the saturation of DNA
witha/b-type small acid soluble proteins.
16,20
The spores ofC. difﬁcilehas the innermost spore
compartment known as the spore core, which contains the
spore DNA, RNA and most enzymes.
16
The spore core is
encased in three protective layers: the ﬁrst is the com-
pressed inner membrane protein surrounded by the germ
cell wall, which has a very low permeability to small mol-
ecules, including water, and protects the core from DNA-
damaging molecules, the second is the peptidoglycan cor-
tex, a coat that predominantly consists of proteins, and the
third is the exosporium (the outermost layer), which pre-
dominantly consists of glycoproteins.
16
During CDI,C. difﬁcileinitiates a sporulation pathway
that produces dormant spores that lead to persistence and
dissemination of CDI within hospitalized patients, and the
pathway is triggered by environmental stimuli such as
nutrient starvation, quorum sensing and other unidentiﬁed
stress factors.
16,17
WhenC. difﬁcilespores are ingested,
the spores are capable of enduring the acidic conditions of
the stomach and then transition to a metabolically active
state (germinate) in the small intestine.
21
Germination of
C. difﬁcilespores and the growth of vegetative forms take
place only in the lower gastrointestinal tract where the
oxygen concentration is very low.
22,23
Some contents of the
intestine, such as bile acids, induce germination of the
spores into an actively replicating vegetative cell.
23,24
Taurocholate, a conjugated primary bile acid in the small
intestine, has the ability to promote germination and to
inﬂuence vegetative growth ofC. difﬁcile; in contrast,
chenodeoxycholate, another primary bile acid, inhibits
spore germination inC. difﬁcileand acts both as a
competitive inhibitor of taurocholate and a suppressor of
vegetative growth.
24,25
The efﬁciency of germination varies
between clinical strains ofC. difﬁcileand whether it is
associated with ribotype, disease severity or therapeutic
failure needs further investigation.
23,26
Rationale of the implication of spore inhibition
for the prevention of recurrence ofC. difﬁcile
infection: is it the absolute and only solution?
Recurrence is a problematic issue in CDI, with 20e30% of
patients facing at least one episode of recurrence even
when treated with a therapeutic drug of choice for CDI.
21,27
In a simulated CDI gut model, although vancomycin suc-
cessfully treated the initial episode of CDI, recurrence
occurred approximately 18 days after therapy cessation, in
which the germination of spores ofC. difﬁcilein the envi-
ronment of a bioﬁlm was noted.
28
The recurrence rates of
clinical patients with CDI receiving metronidazole and
vancomycin therapy, two of the most commonly used anti-
C. difﬁcileantibiotics, were 27.1% and 24.0%, respec-
tively.
27
The recurrence could be due to either reinfection

of a susceptible individual or reactivation of latent spores
within the individualÕs gastrointestinal tract.
27
CDI recurrence has a multi-factorial complex mecha-
nism, but gut microbiota disruption coincident with viable
C. difÞcilespores is considered as the most important
factor.
28,29
Of course, targeting spores ofC. difÞcileis not
the only way to resolve the troublesome CDI recurrence
problem; multiple factors, including gut microbiota status
and the ribotype of theC. difÞcile(with different spore
germination efÞciency) also inßuences the recurrence rate
of CDI.
26
For example, rifaximin, though lacking spore-
inhibiting effects, can prevent the recurrence of CDI
when given immediately after completing standard anti-CDI
antibiotics through its relative sparing of enteric micro-
biota.
30e32
The ribotype ofC. difÞcilewith different spore
germination efÞciencies will inßuence the recurrent rate of
CDI; for example, ribotype 027 isolates exhibit signiÞcantly
higher germination efÞciencies in the presence of sodium
taurocholate than ribotype 106 and ribotype 078.
26
Even with the inßuence of the gut microbiota condition
and the ribotype of CDI, developing antimicrobial agents
with both anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects
have been proven to provide a way to not only treat CDI
but also prevent its recurrence, including Þdaxomicin, one
of the drugs of choice for CDI, and cadazolid and rid-
inilazole, two antimicrobial agents still in phase II clinical
trials (Table 1).
33e37
The application of the spore-inhibiting effect
of current anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agents
in the therapy ofC. difÞcileinfection and its
recurrence
The effectiveness of an anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agent
toward CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect on spores
ofC. difÞcileand vice versa.
38e40
Though many antimi-
crobial agents are regarded as drugs of choice for CDI, such
as Þdaxomicin and vancomycin, their inhibitory effects on
C. difÞcilespores are diverse, which might be due to their
different adherent and inhibitory effects toward spores of
C. difÞcile
38,39
; in contrast, tigecycline and piperacillin/
tazobactam, two commonly used antimicrobial agents in
the clinic, both have a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on
spore production at subminimum inhibitory concentrations
(sub-MICs) in-vitro, but their clinical application is limited
because of their inadequate therapeutic effect on
CDI.
16,40,41
If an antimicrobial agent, such as Þdaxomicin,
has both anti-vegetative cell and anti-spore effects toward
C. difÞcile, it is assumed to be able to not only achieve a
therapeutic effect but also lower the recurrence rate.
33
In
contrast, if an antimicrobial agent, such as vancomycin, has
only anti-vegetative cell effects but lacks anti-spore effects
towardC. difÞcile, it will be hypothetically only achieving a
therapeutic effect but with a possible high recurrence rate
after therapy unless there is some modiÞcation of the
antimicrobial agents to strengthen its effect on spores.
38,39
Fidaxomicin, a drug used for CDI therapy, can inhibit both
the sporulation and the outgrowth of a vegetative cell from
the germinating spore, but its effect on the germination of
C. difÞcilespores is limited (Table 1).
30,42e45
Fidaxomicin
has a persistent inhibitory effect on sporulation when addedto early-stationary-phase cells inC. difÞcilestrains,
including the epidemic NAP1/BI/027 strain at sub-MICs, and
thus prevents subsequent growth and toxin production in-
vitro; in contrast, vancomycin and metronidazole do not
inhibit sporulation at similar sub-MICs.
30,43,44
In contrast to
its inhibitory effect on sporulation, Þdaxomicin was found to
have no inhibitory effect on the initiation ofC. difÞcile
spore germination by analyzing the kinetics of the initiation
of spore germination.
42
The spore-inhibiting effect of Þdaxomicin has been
illustrated in clinical trials, although the clinical cure rates
with Þdaxomicin were similar to those with vancomycin in
both the modiÞed intention-to-treat analysis (88.2% with
Þdaxomicin and 85.8% with vancomycin) and per-protocol
analysis (92.1% and 89.8%, respectively), signiÞcantly fewer
patients in the Þdaxomicin group than in the vancomycin
group had a recurrence of the infection, in both the modi-
Þed intention-to-treat analysis (15.4%vs.25.3%,PZ0.005)
and per-protocol analysis (13.3%vs.24.0%,PZ0.004).
46
The lower recurrence rate following Þdaxomicin therapy
compared to vancomycin was also due to its lower effect on
the microbiota.
15,47e50
In the mice model, Þdaxomicin
reduced the proportion of Clostridial growth to a lesser
extent, but increased that of Bacteroidia, resulting in less
disturbance in microbiota diversity.
47
The lesser inßuence
on the microbiota composition of Þdaxomicin, compared to
vancomycin, promoted faster microbial recovery in the gut,
and had more colonization resistance toC. difÞcile.
48e50
Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been pro-
posed as a possible way of inhibiting spores; as a result,
redesigning anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agents with the
ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another
pathway for the development of anti-C. difÞcilespore
agents.
38,39
Vancomycin, although considered as one of the
drugs of choice for CDI, was found to have no inhibitory
effect on the initiation ofC. difÞcilespore germination by
analyzing the kinetics of the initiation of spore germina-
tion.
42
Thus, the recurrence rate after vancomycin therapy
was as high as 24.0%.
27
although vancomycin itself has no
effect onC. difÞcilespores, a vancomycin-loaded spore-
targeting iron oxide nanoparticle (van-IONP) that selec-
tively binds toC. difÞcilespores has been developed to
successfully delay spore germination.
38
Potential future armament for inhibitingC.
difÞcilespores and preventing recurrence of
C. difÞcileinfection
Some antimicrobial agents undergoing clinical trials have
shown excellent anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects,
which can not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence
(Table 1).
33e37
Cadazolid, a novel ßuoroquinolone-
oxazolidinone antibiotic in phase II and III trials currently,
exhibits potent in-vitro activity againstC. difÞcileand its
spores,
33,34
and has limited effect on the gut microßora,
including theB. fragilisgroup andLactobacillusspp.
51,52
The
cure rates of patients with CDI that received 250, 500, or
1000 mg cadazolid twice daily were 76.5%, 80.0%, 68.4%,
respectively, compared to 68.2% in the group treated with
125 mg vancomycin four times daily; in addition, each
dosage of cadazolid resulted in a lower recurrence rate than

33
It is a pity
in phase III study cadazolid did not achieve its primary

51
Nevertheless
pooling the data from two studies with three randomized
controlled trials, cadazolid revealed no signiÞcantly differ-
ence in sustained clinical response at clinical follow-up
(pooled odds ratio (OR)Z1.14;PZ0.27) but lower recur-
rence rate (pooled ORZ0.71;PZ0.04) compared to
vancomycin.
53
Ridinilazole, a novel class of heterocyclic antibacterial
drugs, can inhibit DNA bacterial synthesis and thus inhibit
the growth ofC. difÞcile.
36,53
Treatment with supra-MIC
concentrations (4and 40MIC) of ridinilazole resulted
in a signiÞcant reduction in vegetative cells over 72 h (4 log
difference,P<0.01) compared with controls without
inducing spore formation.
36,54
Ridinilazole, compared tovancomycin, had almost no effect on the gut microbiota,
including several Bacteroidaceae and Clostridiaceae fam-
ilies, and maintained the intestinal bile acid proÞle.
35,55
In
phase II trials, the sustained clinical response in patients in
the ridinilazole group was 66.7%, which was superior to that
of 42.4% in the vancomycin group.
35
Of note, the recurrence
rate of CDI among patients receiving ridinilazole was 14.3%,
which was lower than that of 34.8% for vancomycin.
35
Ramoplanin, a glycolipodepsipeptide antibiotic that is
active againstC. difÞcile, results in spore counts consis-
tently below the level of detection for 28 days after even a
brief (30-min) exposure in-vitro.
39

tigating exposure to ramoplanin, an increase in spore counts
was noted after removal of theC. difÞcileexosporium,
which suggests that rather than being directly sporicidal,
ramoplanin adheres to the exosporium for a prolonged

In hamster models of CDI,C. difÞcile
spores were recovered signiÞcantly more often from the
cecal contents of vancomycin-treated hamsters (nZ19/23)
compared with ramoplanin-treated (nZ6/23) hamsters
(P<0.05).
37
It is unfortunate that though ramoplanin
revealed inhibitory effects onC. difÞcileand its spores in-
vitro, its clinical efÞcacy toward CDI and its recurrence is
still lacking.
32
CRS3123, a fully synthetic diaryldiamine antimicrobial
drug, prevents bothC. difÞcilegrowth and spore produc-
tion by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, with a>10-
fold reduction in the sporulation rate in-vitro.
56
To date,
only data from a phase I study assessing the safety and
tolerability of CRS3123 are available, and evidence of its
clinical effect on CDI and its recurrence is deÞcient.
32
Nisin, a bacteriocin produced by several strains ofLac-
tococcus lactis, was noted to have inhibitory activity
against clinical isolates ofC. difÞcile, with spore viability
reduced by 40e50% in-vitro.
57
However, in-vivo evidence of
nisin in treating CDI or its recurrence is absent.
Development of a vaccine targeting the spores ofC.
difÞcileprovides a feasible pathway for preventing CDI
recurrence.
58
Anti-spore IgY from chickens delayed the
occurrence of diarrhea by 1.5 d and the spore adherence to
the colonic mucosa by 90% in a mouse model, and co-
administration of anti-spore IgY coupled with vancomycin
delayed the appearance of recurrent diarrhea by a median
of 2 days.
58
Some small molecules and compounds were noted to
have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but a determination
of their ÒrealÓ clinical efÞcacy needs further clinical tri-
als.
59,60
Carvacrol, a food-grade, plant-derived compound,
signiÞcantly reduces sporulation, germination and spore
outgrowth ofC. difÞcileand downregulates critical genes
involved in spore production in-vitro.
59
Rhodomyrtone, a
bioactive compound derived from the leaves of the rose
myrtle (Rhodomyrtus tomentosa), is four-fold more potent
than vancomycin in inhibitingC. difÞcilespore outgrowth
in-vitro.
60
Conclusion
Developing an antimicrobial agent with a good inhibitory
effect on bothC. difÞcilevegetative cells and spores can
be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its
recurrence, such as Þdaxomicin. Cadazolid and ridinilazole
possess a spore-inhibiting effect in-vitro, and thus decrease
the recurrence of CDI after cessation of the drug in phase II
and III clinical trials. Some small molecules and compounds
were noted to have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but the
determination of their ÒrealÓ clinical efÞcacy requires
further clinical trials.

AbstractClostridioides difÞcileis one of the most common nosocomial gastrointestinal
pathogens, and recurrence is a problematic issue because approximately 20e30% of patients
experience at least one episode of recurrence, even after treatment with a therapeutic drug
of choice forC. difÞcileinfection (CDI), such as vancomycin. CDI recurrence has a multifacto-
rial complex mechanism, in which gut microbiota disruption coincident with viableC. difÞcile
spores, is considered the most important factor. The effectiveness of an anti-C. difÞcileanti-
microbial agent against CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect onC. difÞcilespores and
vice versa. However, an antimicrobial agent, such as Þdaxomicin, which has a good inhibitory
effect on bothC. difÞcilevegetative cells and spores is assumed to not only treat CDI but also
prevent its recurrence. Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been proposed as a
possible mechanism of inhibiting spores, and as a result, redesigning anti-C. difÞcileantimicro-
bial agents with the ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another pathway for the
development of anti-C. difÞcilespore agents. For example, vancomycin lacks an inhibitory ef-
fect againstC. difÞcilespores, but a vancomycin-loaded spore-targeting iron oxide nanopar-
ticle that selectively binds toC. difÞcilespores has been developed to successfully delay
spore germination. Some new antimicrobial agents in phase II clinical trials, including cadazo-
lid and ridinilazole, have shown exceptional anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects that
can be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence in the future.

Introduction
Clostridioides difﬁcileis one of the most common nosoco-
mial gastrointestinal pathogens, with clinical presentations
ranging from mild diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis
to toxic megacolon, with a mortality of up to 25e40%.
1e9
Severe colitis develops in approximately 3% of patients
withC. difﬁcileinfection (CDI) who may have paradoxical
decrease in the amount of diarrhea after ileus or toxic
megacolon developed.
3,10
Diagnosis of CDI relies on the
detection of toxigenicC. difﬁcile, its toxins or toxin genes
in stool.
9,11
Metronidazole was suggested for mild CDI and vanco-
mycin was recommended for severe CDI.
8
Nevertheless,
oral vancomycin and ﬁdaxomicin have been suggested to
replace metronidazole as the therapeutic choice for either
mild-moderate or severe CDI in the Clinical Practice
Guidelines forC. difﬁcileInfection in Adults and Children:
2017 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America
(IDSA) and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America
(SHEA).
12
For patients with severe and fulminant forms of
CDI presenting as ileus, oral intake of vancomycin or
ﬁdaxomicin is disrupted because of the obstruction of the
gut because ﬁdaxomicin can only be administered orally;
and vancomycin, either administered orally or intra-
rectally. This leads to marked disruption of the microbiota,
leading to prolonged loss of colonization resistance toC.
difﬁcileand dense colonization by vancomycin-resistant
Enterococcus,K. pneumoniae, andE. coli.
13
Although antimicrobial resistance is not clinically prob-
lematic, treating CDI with metronidazole and vancomycin is
associated with a high treatment failure rate and high
relapse rate.
14
According to the Clinical Practice Guidelines
by IDSA/SHEA, oral vancomycin was still the drug of choice
for recurrentC. difﬁcileassociated diarrhea, but the rate
of second recurrence rate is as high as 22.6e41.8%, despite
successful treatment with vancomycin.
15
The high recur-
rence rate of CDI after treatment might be due to the
generation of spores that lead to persistence of CDI.
16,17
The biology of spores in the pathogenesis ofC.
difﬁcile
Owing to its strict anaerobic requirements, the infectious
and transmissible morphotype ofC. difﬁcileis a dormant
spore, which is characterized by resistance to heat, oxy-
gen, and common disinfectants, such as ethanol-based
hand sanitizers.
16,18,19
The sporeeresistance properties
are attributed to a low water content (25e60% of wet
weight), elevated levels of dipicolonic acid (25% of core dry
weight) chelated with calcium, and the saturation of DNA
witha/b-type small acid soluble proteins.
16,20
The spores ofC. difﬁcilehas the innermost spore
compartment known as the spore core, which contains the
spore DNA, RNA and most enzymes.
16
The spore core is
encased in three protective layers: the ﬁrst is the com-
pressed inner membrane protein surrounded by the germ
cell wall, which has a very low permeability to small mol-
ecules, including water, and protects the core from DNA-
damaging molecules, the second is the peptidoglycan cor-
tex, a coat that predominantly consists of proteins, and the
third is the exosporium (the outermost layer), which pre-
dominantly consists of glycoproteins.
16
During CDI,C. difﬁcileinitiates a sporulation pathway
that produces dormant spores that lead to persistence and
dissemination of CDI within hospitalized patients, and the
pathway is triggered by environmental stimuli such as
nutrient starvation, quorum sensing and other unidentiﬁed
stress factors.
16,17
WhenC. difﬁcilespores are ingested,
the spores are capable of enduring the acidic conditions of
the stomach and then transition to a metabolically active
state (germinate) in the small intestine.
21
Germination of
C. difﬁcilespores and the growth of vegetative forms take
place only in the lower gastrointestinal tract where the
oxygen concentration is very low.
22,23
Some contents of the
intestine, such as bile acids, induce germination of the
spores into an actively replicating vegetative cell.
23,24
Taurocholate, a conjugated primary bile acid in the small
intestine, has the ability to promote germination and to
inﬂuence vegetative growth ofC. difﬁcile; in contrast,
chenodeoxycholate, another primary bile acid, inhibits
spore germination inC. difﬁcileand acts both as a
competitive inhibitor of taurocholate and a suppressor of
vegetative growth.
24,25
The efﬁciency of germination varies
between clinical strains ofC. difﬁcileand whether it is
associated with ribotype, disease severity or therapeutic
failure needs further investigation.
23,26
Rationale of the implication of spore inhibition
for the prevention of recurrence ofC. difﬁcile
infection: is it the absolute and only solution?
Recurrence is a problematic issue in CDI, with 20e30% of
patients facing at least one episode of recurrence even
when treated with a therapeutic drug of choice for CDI.
21,27
In a simulated CDI gut model, although vancomycin suc-
cessfully treated the initial episode of CDI, recurrence
occurred approximately 18 days after therapy cessation, in
which the germination of spores ofC. difﬁcilein the envi-
ronment of a bioﬁlm was noted.
28
The recurrence rates of
clinical patients with CDI receiving metronidazole and
vancomycin therapy, two of the most commonly used anti-
C. difﬁcileantibiotics, were 27.1% and 24.0%, respec-
tively.
27
The recurrence could be due to either reinfection

1012

of a susceptible individual or reactivation of latent spores
within the individualÕs gastrointestinal tract.
27
CDI recurrence has a multi-factorial complex mecha-
nism, but gut microbiota disruption coincident with viable
C. difÞcilespores is considered as the most important
factor.
28,29
Of course, targeting spores ofC. difÞcileis not
the only way to resolve the troublesome CDI recurrence
problem; multiple factors, including gut microbiota status
and the ribotype of theC. difÞcile(with different spore
germination efÞciency) also inßuences the recurrence rate
of CDI.
26
For example, rifaximin, though lacking spore-
inhibiting effects, can prevent the recurrence of CDI
when given immediately after completing standard anti-CDI
antibiotics through its relative sparing of enteric micro-
biota.
30e32
The ribotype ofC. difÞcilewith different spore
germination efÞciencies will inßuence the recurrent rate of
CDI; for example, ribotype 027 isolates exhibit signiÞcantly
higher germination efÞciencies in the presence of sodium
taurocholate than ribotype 106 and ribotype 078.
26
Even with the inßuence of the gut microbiota condition
and the ribotype of CDI, developing antimicrobial agents
with both anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects
have been proven to provide a way to not only treat CDI
but also prevent its recurrence, including Þdaxomicin, one
of the drugs of choice for CDI, and cadazolid and rid-
inilazole, two antimicrobial agents still in phase II clinical
trials (Table 1).
33e37
The application of the spore-inhibiting effect
of current anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agents
in the therapy ofC. difÞcileinfection and its
recurrence
The effectiveness of an anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agent
toward CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect on spores
ofC. difÞcileand vice versa.
38e40
Though many antimi-
crobial agents are regarded as drugs of choice for CDI, such
as Þdaxomicin and vancomycin, their inhibitory effects on
C. difÞcilespores are diverse, which might be due to their
different adherent and inhibitory effects toward spores of
C. difÞcile
38,39
; in contrast, tigecycline and piperacillin/
tazobactam, two commonly used antimicrobial agents in
the clinic, both have a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on
spore production at subminimum inhibitory concentrations
(sub-MICs) in-vitro, but their clinical application is limited
because of their inadequate therapeutic effect on
CDI.
16,40,41
If an antimicrobial agent, such as Þdaxomicin,
has both anti-vegetative cell and anti-spore effects toward
C. difÞcile, it is assumed to be able to not only achieve a
therapeutic effect but also lower the recurrence rate.
33
In
contrast, if an antimicrobial agent, such as vancomycin, has
only anti-vegetative cell effects but lacks anti-spore effects
towardC. difÞcile, it will be hypothetically only achieving a
therapeutic effect but with a possible high recurrence rate
after therapy unless there is some modiÞcation of the
antimicrobial agents to strengthen its effect on spores.
38,39
Fidaxomicin, a drug used for CDI therapy, can inhibit both
the sporulation and the outgrowth of a vegetative cell from
the germinating spore, but its effect on the germination of
C. difÞcilespores is limited (Table 1).
30,42e45
Fidaxomicin
has a persistent inhibitory effect on sporulation when addedto early-stationary-phase cells inC. difÞcilestrains,
including the epidemic NAP1/BI/027 strain at sub-MICs, and
thus prevents subsequent growth and toxin production in-
vitro; in contrast, vancomycin and metronidazole do not
inhibit sporulation at similar sub-MICs.
30,43,44
In contrast to
its inhibitory effect on sporulation, Þdaxomicin was found to
have no inhibitory effect on the initiation ofC. difÞcile
spore germination by analyzing the kinetics of the initiation
of spore germination.
42
The spore-inhibiting effect of Þdaxomicin has been
illustrated in clinical trials, although the clinical cure rates
with Þdaxomicin were similar to those with vancomycin in
both the modiÞed intention-to-treat analysis (88.2% with
Þdaxomicin and 85.8% with vancomycin) and per-protocol
analysis (92.1% and 89.8%, respectively), signiÞcantly fewer
patients in the Þdaxomicin group than in the vancomycin
group had a recurrence of the infection, in both the modi-
Þed intention-to-treat analysis (15.4%vs.25.3%,PZ0.005)
and per-protocol analysis (13.3%vs.24.0%,PZ0.004).
46
The lower recurrence rate following Þdaxomicin therapy
compared to vancomycin was also due to its lower effect on
the microbiota.
15,47e50
In the mice model, Þdaxomicin
reduced the proportion of Clostridial growth to a lesser
extent, but increased that of Bacteroidia, resulting in less
disturbance in microbiota diversity.
47
The lesser inßuence
on the microbiota composition of Þdaxomicin, compared to
vancomycin, promoted faster microbial recovery in the gut,
and had more colonization resistance toC. difÞcile.
48e50
Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been pro-
posed as a possible way of inhibiting spores; as a result,
redesigning anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agents with the
ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another
pathway for the development of anti-C. difÞcilespore
agents.
38,39
Vancomycin, although considered as one of the
drugs of choice for CDI, was found to have no inhibitory
effect on the initiation ofC. difÞcilespore germination by
analyzing the kinetics of the initiation of spore germina-
tion.
42
Thus, the recurrence rate after vancomycin therapy
was as high as 24.0%.
27

Conclusion
Developing an antimicrobial agent with a good inhibitory
effect on bothC. difÞcilevegetative cells and spores can
be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its
recurrence, such as Þdaxomicin. Cadazolid and ridinilazole
possess a spore-inhibiting effect in-vitro, and thus decrease
the recurrence of CDI after cessation of the drug in phase II
and III clinical trials. Some small molecules and compounds
were noted to have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but the
determination of their ÒrealÓ clinical efÞcacy requires
further clinical trials.

AbstractClostridioides difÞcileis one of the most common nosocomial gastrointestinal
pathogens, and recurrence is a problematic issue because approximately 20e30% of patients
experience at least one episode of recurrence, even after treatment with a therapeutic drug
of choice forC. difÞcileinfection (CDI), such as vancomycin. CDI recurrence has a multifacto-
rial complex mechanism, in which gut microbiota disruption coincident with viableC. difÞcile
spores, is considered the most important factor. The effectiveness of an anti-C. difÞcileanti-
microbial agent against CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect onC. difÞcilespores and
vice versa. However, an antimicrobial agent, such as Þdaxomicin, which has a good inhibitory
effect on bothC. difÞcilevegetative cells and spores is assumed to not only treat CDI but also
prevent its recurrence. Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been proposed as a
possible mechanism of inhibiting spores, and as a result, redesigning anti-C. difÞcileantimicro-
bial agents with the ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another pathway for the
development of anti-C. difÞcilespore agents. For example, vancomycin lacks an inhibitory ef-
fect againstC. difÞcilespores, but a vancomycin-loaded spore-targeting iron oxide nanopar-
ticle that selectively binds toC. difÞcilespores has been developed to successfully delay
spore germination. Some new antimicrobial agents in phase II clinical trials, including cadazo-
lid and ridinilazole, have shown exceptional anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects that
can be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence in the future.

Introduction
Clostridioides difﬁcileis one of the most common nosoco-
mial gastrointestinal pathogens, with clinical presentations
ranging from mild diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis
to toxic megacolon, with a mortality of up to 25e40%.
1e9
Severe colitis develops in approximately 3% of patients
withC. difﬁcileinfection (CDI) who may have paradoxical
decrease in the amount of diarrhea after ileus or toxic
megacolon developed.
3,10
Diagnosis of CDI relies on the
detection of toxigenicC. difﬁcile, its toxins or toxin genes
in stool.
9,11
Metronidazole was suggested for mild CDI and vanco-
mycin was recommended for severe CDI.
8
Nevertheless,
oral vancomycin and ﬁdaxomicin have been suggested to
replace metronidazole as the therapeutic choice for either
mild-moderate or severe CDI in the Clinical Practice
Guidelines forC. difﬁcileInfection in Adults and Children:
2017 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America
(IDSA) and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America
(SHEA).
12
For patients with severe and fulminant forms of
CDI presenting as ileus, oral intake of vancomycin or
ﬁdaxomicin is disrupted because of the obstruction of the
gut because ﬁdaxomicin can only be administered orally;
and vancomycin, either administered orally or intra-
rectally. This leads to marked disruption of the microbiota,
leading to prolonged loss of colonization resistance toC.
difﬁcileand dense colonization by vancomycin-resistant
Enterococcus,K. pneumoniae, andE. coli.
13
Although antimicrobial resistance is not clinically prob-
lematic, treating CDI with metronidazole and vancomycin is
associated with a high treatment failure rate and high
relapse rate.
14
According to the Clinical Practice Guidelines
by IDSA/SHEA, oral vancomycin was still the drug of choice
for recurrentC. difﬁcileassociated diarrhea, but the rate
of second recurrence rate is as high as 22.6e41.8%, despite
successful treatment with vancomycin.
15
The high recur-
rence rate of CDI after treatment might be due to the
generation of spores that lead to persistence of CDI.
16,17
The biology of spores in the pathogenesis ofC.
difﬁcile
Owing to its strict anaerobic requirements, the infectious
and transmissible morphotype ofC. difﬁcileis a dormant
spore, which is characterized by resistance to heat, oxy-
gen, and common disinfectants, such as ethanol-based
hand sanitizers.
16,18,19
The sporeeresistance properties
are attributed to a low water content (25e60% of wet
weight), elevated levels of dipicolonic acid (25% of core dry
weight) chelated with calcium, and the saturation of DNA
witha/b-type small acid soluble proteins.
16,20
The spores ofC. difﬁcilehas the innermost spore
compartment known as the spore core, which contains the
spore DNA, RNA and most enzymes.
16
The spore core is
encased in three protective layers: the ﬁrst is the com-
pressed inner membrane protein surrounded by the germ
cell wall, which has a very low permeability to small mol-
ecules, including water, and protects the core from DNA-
damaging molecules, the second is the peptidoglycan cor-
tex, a coat that predominantly consists of proteins, and the
third is the exosporium (the outermost layer), which pre-
dominantly consists of glycoproteins.
16
During CDI,C. difﬁcileinitiates a sporulation pathway
that produces dormant spores that lead to persistence and
dissemination of CDI within hospitalized patients, and the
pathway is triggered by environmental stimuli such as
nutrient starvation, quorum sensing and other unidentiﬁed
stress factors.
16,17
WhenC. difﬁcilespores are ingested,
the spores are capable of enduring the acidic conditions of
the stomach and then transition to a metabolically active
state (germinate) in the small intestine.
21
Germination of
C. difﬁcilespores and the growth of vegetative forms take
place only in the lower gastrointestinal tract where the
oxygen concentration is very low.
22,23
Some contents of the
intestine, such as bile acids, induce germination of the
spores into an actively replicating vegetative cell.
23,24
Taurocholate, a conjugated primary bile acid in the small
intestine, has the ability to promote germination and to
inﬂuence vegetative growth ofC. difﬁcile; in contrast,
chenodeoxycholate, another primary bile acid, inhibits
spore germination inC. difﬁcileand acts both as a
competitive inhibitor of taurocholate and a suppressor of
vegetative growth.
24,25
The efﬁciency of germination varies
between clinical strains ofC. difﬁcileand whether it is
associated with ribotype, disease severity or therapeutic
failure needs further investigation.
23,26
Rationale of the implication of spore inhibition
for the prevention of recurrence ofC. difﬁcile
infection: is it the absolute and only solution?
Recurrence is a problematic issue in CDI, with 20e30% of
patients facing at least one episode of recurrence even
when treated with a therapeutic drug of choice for CDI.
21,27
In a simulated CDI gut model, although vancomycin suc-
cessfully treated the initial episode of CDI, recurrence
occurred approximately 18 days after therapy cessation, in
which the germination of spores ofC. difﬁcilein the envi-
ronment of a bioﬁlm was noted.
28
The recurrence rates of
clinical patients with CDI receiving metronidazole and
vancomycin therapy, two of the most commonly used anti-
C. difﬁcileantibiotics, were 27.1% and 24.0%, respec-
tively.
27
The recurrence could be due to either reinfection
