of a susceptible individual or reactivation of latent spores
within the individualÕs gastrointestinal tract.
27
CDI recurrence has a multi-factorial complex mecha-
nism, but gut microbiota disruption coincident with viable
C. difÞcilespores is considered as the most important
factor.
28,29
Of course, targeting spores ofC. difÞcileis not
the only way to resolve the troublesome CDI recurrence
problem; multiple factors, including gut microbiota status
and the ribotype of theC. difÞcile(with different spore
germination efÞciency) also inßuences the recurrence rate
of CDI.
26
For example, rifaximin, though lacking spore-
inhibiting effects, can prevent the recurrence of CDI
when given immediately after completing standard anti-CDI
antibiotics through its relative sparing of enteric micro-
biota.
30e32
The ribotype ofC. difÞcilewith different spore
germination efÞciencies will inßuence the recurrent rate of
CDI; for example, ribotype 027 isolates exhibit signiÞcantly
higher germination efÞciencies in the presence of sodium
taurocholate than ribotype 106 and ribotype 078.
26
Even with the inßuence of the gut microbiota condition
and the ribotype of CDI, developing antimicrobial agents
with both anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects
have been proven to provide a way to not only treat CDI
but also prevent its recurrence, including Þdaxomicin, one
of the drugs of choice for CDI, and cadazolid and rid-
inilazole, two antimicrobial agents still in phase II clinical
trials (Table 1).
33e37
The application of the spore-inhibiting effect
of current anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agents
in the therapy ofC. difÞcileinfection and its
recurrence
The effectiveness of an anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agent
toward CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect on spores
ofC. difÞcileand vice versa.
38e40
Though many antimi-
crobial agents are regarded as drugs of choice for CDI, such
as Þdaxomicin and vancomycin, their inhibitory effects on
C. difÞcilespores are diverse, which might be due to their
different adherent and inhibitory effects toward spores of
C. difÞcile
38,39
; in contrast, tigecycline and piperacillin/
tazobactam, two commonly used antimicrobial agents in
the clinic, both have a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on
spore production at subminimum inhibitory concentrations
(sub-MICs) in-vitro, but their clinical application is limited
because of their inadequate therapeutic effect on
CDI.
16,40,41
If an antimicrobial agent, such as Þdaxomicin,
has both anti-vegetative cell and anti-spore effects toward
C. difÞcile, it is assumed to be able to not only achieve a
therapeutic effect but also lower the recurrence rate.
33
In
contrast, if an antimicrobial agent, such as vancomycin, has
only anti-vegetative cell effects but lacks anti-spore effects
towardC. difÞcile, it will be hypothetically only achieving a
therapeutic effect but with a possible high recurrence rate
after therapy unless there is some modiÞcation of the
antimicrobial agents to strengthen its effect on spores.
38,39
Fidaxomicin, a drug used for CDI therapy, can inhibit both
the sporulation and the outgrowth of a vegetative cell from
the germinating spore, but its effect on the germination of
C. difÞcilespores is limited (Table 1).
30,42e45
Fidaxomicin
has a persistent inhibitory effect on sporulation when addedto early-stationary-phase cells inC. difÞcilestrains,
including the epidemic NAP1/BI/027 strain at sub-MICs, and
thus prevents subsequent growth and toxin production in-
vitro; in contrast, vancomycin and metronidazole do not
inhibit sporulation at similar sub-MICs.
30,43,44
In contrast to
its inhibitory effect on sporulation, Þdaxomicin was found to
have no inhibitory effect on the initiation ofC. difÞcile
spore germination by analyzing the kinetics of the initiation
of spore germination.
42
The spore-inhibiting effect of Þdaxomicin has been
illustrated in clinical trials, although the clinical cure rates
with Þdaxomicin were similar to those with vancomycin in
both the modiÞed intention-to-treat analysis (88.2% with
Þdaxomicin and 85.8% with vancomycin) and per-protocol
analysis (92.1% and 89.8%, respectively), signiÞcantly fewer
patients in the Þdaxomicin group than in the vancomycin
group had a recurrence of the infection, in both the modi-
Þed intention-to-treat analysis (15.4%vs.25.3%,PZ0.005)
and per-protocol analysis (13.3%vs.24.0%,PZ0.004).
46
The lower recurrence rate following Þdaxomicin therapy
compared to vancomycin was also due to its lower effect on
the microbiota.
15,47e50
In the mice model, Þdaxomicin
reduced the proportion of Clostridial growth to a lesser
extent, but increased that of Bacteroidia, resulting in less
disturbance in microbiota diversity.
47
The lesser inßuence
on the microbiota composition of Þdaxomicin, compared to
vancomycin, promoted faster microbial recovery in the gut,
and had more colonization resistance toC. difÞcile.
48e50
Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been pro-
posed as a possible way of inhibiting spores; as a result,
redesigning anti-C. difÞcileantimicrobial agents with the
ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another
pathway for the development of anti-C. difÞcilespore
agents.
38,39
Vancomycin, although considered as one of the
drugs of choice for CDI, was found to have no inhibitory
effect on the initiation ofC. difÞcilespore germination by
analyzing the kinetics of the initiation of spore germina-
tion.
42
Thus, the recurrence rate after vancomycin therapy
was as high as 24.0%.
27
although vancomycin itself has no
effect onC. difÞcilespores, a vancomycin-loaded spore-
targeting iron oxide nanoparticle (van-IONP) that selec-
tively binds toC. difÞcilespores has been developed to
successfully delay spore germination.
38
Potential future armament for inhibitingC.
difÞcilespores and preventing recurrence of
C. difÞcileinfection
Some antimicrobial agents undergoing clinical trials have
shown excellent anti-C. difÞcileand spore-inhibiting effects,
which can not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence
(Table 1).
33e37
Cadazolid, a novel ßuoroquinolone-
oxazolidinone antibiotic in phase II and III trials currently,
exhibits potent in-vitro activity againstC. difÞcileand its
spores,
33,34
and has limited effect on the gut microßora,
including theB. fragilisgroup andLactobacillusspp.
51,52
The
cure rates of patients with CDI that received 250, 500, or
1000 mg cadazolid twice daily were 76.5%, 80.0%, 68.4%,
respectively, compared to 68.2% in the group treated with
125 mg vancomycin four times daily; in addition, each
dosage of cadazolid resulted in a lower recurrence rate than

33
It is a pity
in phase III study cadazolid did not achieve its primary
endpoint of non-inferiority to vancomycin for clinical cure in
oneoftwophaseIIIC difÞcileinfection trials.
51
Nevertheless
pooling the data from two studies with three randomized
controlled trials, cadazolid revealed no signiÞcantly differ-
ence in sustained clinical response at clinical follow-up
(pooled odds ratio (OR)Z1.14;PZ0.27) but lower recur-
rence rate (pooled ORZ0.71;PZ0.04) compared to
vancomycin.
53
Ridinilazole, a novel class of heterocyclic antibacterial
drugs, can inhibit DNA bacterial synthesis and thus inhibit
the growth ofC. difÞcile.
36,53
Treatment with supra-MIC
concentrations (4and 40MIC) of ridinilazole resulted
in a signiÞcant reduction in vegetative cells over 72 h (4 log
difference,P<0.01) compared with controls without
inducing spore formation.
36,54
Ridinilazole, compared tovancomycin, had almost no effect on the gut microbiota,
including several Bacteroidaceae and Clostridiaceae fam-
ilies, and maintained the intestinal bile acid proÞle.
35,55
In
phase II trials, the sustained clinical response in patients in
the ridinilazole group was 66.7%, which was superior to that
of 42.4% in the vancomycin group.
35
Of note, the recurrence
rate of CDI among patients receiving ridinilazole was 14.3%,
which was lower than that of 34.8% for vancomycin.
35
Ramoplanin, a glycolipodepsipeptide antibiotic that is
active againstC. difÞcile, results in spore counts consis-
tently below the level of detection for 28 days after even a
brief (30-min) exposure in-vitro.
39

tigating exposure to ramoplanin, an increase in spore counts
was noted after removal of theC. difÞcileexosporium,
which suggests that rather than being directly sporicidal,
ramoplanin adheres to the exosporium for a prolonged

In hamster models of CDI,C. difÞcile
spores were recovered signiÞcantly more often from the
cecal contents of vancomycin-treated hamsters (nZ19/23)
compared with ramoplanin-treated (nZ6/23) hamsters
(P<0.05).
37
It is unfortunate that though ramoplanin
revealed inhibitory effects onC. difÞcileand its spores in-
vitro, its clinical efÞcacy toward CDI and its recurrence is
still lacking.
32
CRS3123, a fully synthetic diaryldiamine antimicrobial
drug, prevents bothC. difÞcilegrowth and spore produc-
tion by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, with a>10-
fold reduction in the sporulation rate in-vitro.
56
To date,
only data from a phase I study assessing the safety and
tolerability of CRS3123 are available, and evidence of its
clinical effect on CDI and its recurrence is deÞcient.
32
Nisin, a bacteriocin produced by several strains ofLac-
tococcus lactis, was noted to have inhibitory activity
against clinical isolates ofC. difÞcile, with spore viability
reduced by 40e50% in-vitro.
57
However, in-vivo evidence of
nisin in treating CDI or its recurrence is absent.
Development of a vaccine targeting the spores ofC.
difÞcileprovides a feasible pathway for preventing CDI
recurrence.
58
Anti-spore IgY from chickens delayed the
occurrence of diarrhea by 1.5 d and the spore adherence to
the colonic mucosa by 90% in a mouse model, and co-
administration of anti-spore IgY coupled with vancomycin
delayed the appearance of recurrent diarrhea by a median
of 2 days.
58
Some small molecules and compounds were noted to
have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but a determination
of their ÒrealÓ clinical efÞcacy needs further clinical tri-
als.
59,60
Carvacrol, a food-grade, plant-derived compound,
signiÞcantly reduces sporulation, germination and spore
outgrowth ofC. difÞcileand downregulates critical genes
involved in spore production in-vitro.
59
Rhodomyrtone, a
bioactive compound derived from the leaves of the rose
myrtle (Rhodomyrtus tomentosa), is four-fold more potent
than vancomycin in inhibitingC. difÞcilespore outgrowth
in-vitro.
60
Conclusion
Developing an antimicrobial agent with a good inhibitory
effect on bothC. difÞcilevegetative cells and spores can
be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its
recurrence, such as Þdaxomicin. Cadazolid and ridinilazole
possess a spore-inhibiting effect in-vitro, and thus decrease
the recurrence of CDI after cessation of the drug in phase II
and III clinical trials. Some small molecules and compounds
were noted to have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but the
determination of their ÒrealÓ clinical efÞcacy requires
further clinical trials.

# Inhibition of spores to prevent the recurrence of *Clostridioides difficile* infection - A possibility or an improbability?

Chun-Wei Chiu<sup>a</sup>, Pei-Jane Tsai<sup>b</sup>, Ching-Chi Lee<sup>c</sup>, Wen-Chien Ko<sup>c,d,\*</sup>, Yuan-Pin Hung<sup>a,c,\*\*</sup>

## Abstract*Clostridioides difficile* is one of the most common nosocomial gastrointestinal pathogens, and recurrence is a problematic issue because approximately20–30% of patients experience at least one episode of recurrence, even after treatment with a therapeutic drug of choice for *C. difficile* infection (CDI), such as vancomycin. CDI recurrence has a multifactorial complex mechanism, in which gut microbiota disruption coincident with viable *C. difficile* spores is considered the most important factor. The effectiveness of an anti-*C. difficile* antimicrobial agent against CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect on *C. difficile* spores and vice versa. However, an antimicrobial agent, such as fidaxomicin, which has a good inhibitory effect on both *C. difficile* vegetative cells and spores is assumed to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence. Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been proposed as a possible mechanism of inhibiting spores, and as a result, redesigning anti-*C. difficile* antimicrobial agents with the ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another pathway for the development of anti-*C. difficile* spore agents. For example, vancomycin lacks an inhibitory effect against *C. difficile* spores, but a vancomycin-loaded spore-targeting iron oxide nanoparticle that selectively binds to *C. difficile* spores has been developed to successfully delay spore germination. Some new antimicrobial agents in phase II clinical trials, including cadazolid and ridinilazole, have shown exceptional anti-*C. difficile* and spore-inhibiting effects that can be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence in the future.

## Introduction*Clostridioides difficile* is one of the most common nosocomial gastrointestinal pathogens, with clinical presentations ranging from mild diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis to toxic megacolon, with a mortality of up to25–40% [1–9]. Severe colitis develops in approximately3% of patients with *C. difficile* infection (CDI) who may have paradoxical decrease in the amount of diarrhea after ileus or toxic megacolon developed [3,10]. Diagnosis of CDI relies on the detection of toxigenic *C. difficile*, its toxins or toxin genes in stool [9,11].

Metronidazole was suggested for mild CDI and vancomycin was recommended for severe CDI [8]. Nevertheless, oral vancomycin and fidaxomicin have been suggested to replace metronidazole as the therapeutic choice for either mild-moderate or severe CDI in the Clinical Practice Guidelines for *C. difficile* Infection in Adults and Children:2017 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA) [12]. For patients with severe and fulminant forms of CDI presenting as ileus, oral intake of vancomycin or fidaxomicin is disrupted because of the obstruction of the gut because fidaxomicin can only be administered orally; and vancomycin, either administered orally or intra-rectally. This leads to marked disruption of the microbiota, leading to prolonged loss of colonization resistance to *C. difficile* and dense colonization by vancomycin-resistant *Enterococcus*, *K. pneumoniae*, and *E. coli* [13].

Although antimicrobial resistance is not clinically problematic, treating CDI with metronidazole and vancomycin is associated with a high treatment failure rate and high relapse rate [14]. According to the Clinical Practice Guidelines by IDSA/SHEA, oral vancomycin was still the drug of choice for recurrent *C. difficile* associated diarrhea, but the rate of second recurrence rate is as high as22.6–41.8%, despite successful treatment with vancomycin [15]. The high recurrence rate of CDI after treatment might be due to the generation of spores that lead to persistence of CDI [16,17].

## The biology of spores in the pathogenesis of *C. difficile*

Owing to its strict anaerobic requirements, the infectious and transmissible morphotype of *C. difficile* is a dormant spore, which is characterized by resistance to heat, oxygen, and common disinfectants, such as ethanol-based hand sanitizers [16,18,19]. The spore resistance properties are attributed to a low water content (25–60% of wet weight), elevated levels of dipicolinic acid (25% of core dry weight) chelated with calcium, and the saturation of DNA with α/β-type small acid soluble proteins [16,20].

The spores of *C. difficile* have the innermost spore compartment known as the spore core, which contains the spore DNA, RNA and most enzymes [16]. The spore core is encased in three protective layers: the first is the compressed inner membrane protein surrounded by the germ cell wall, which has a very low permeability to small molecules, including water, and protects the core from DNA-damaging molecules; the second is the peptidoglycan cortex; a coat that predominantly consists of proteins; and the third is the exosporium (the outermost layer), which predominantly consists of glycoproteins [16].

During CDI, *C. difficile* initiates a sporulation pathway that produces dormant spores that lead to persistence and dissemination of CDI within hospitalized patients, and the pathway is triggered by environmental stimuli such as nutrient starvation, quorum sensing and other unidentified stress factors [16,17]. When *C. difficile* spores are ingested, the spores are capable of enduring the acidic conditions of the stomach and then transition to a metabolically active state (germinate) in the small intestine [21]. Germination of *C. difficile* spores and the growth of vegetative forms take place only in the lower gastrointestinal tract where the oxygen concentration is very low [22,23]. Some contents of the intestine, such as bile acids, induce germination of the spores into an actively replicating vegetative cell [23,24]. Taurocholate, a conjugated primary bile acid in the small intestine, has the ability to promote germination and to influence vegetative growth of *C. difficile*; in contrast, chenodeoxycholate, another primary bile acid, inhibits spore germination in *C. difficile* and acts both as a competitive inhibitor of taurocholate and a suppressor of vegetative growth [24,25]. The efficiency of germination varies between clinical strains of *C. difficile* and whether it is associated with ribotype, disease severity or therapeutic failure needs further investigation [23,26].

## Rationale of the implication of spore inhibition for the prevention of recurrence of *C. difficile* infection: is it the absolute and only solution?

Recurrence is a problematic issue in CDI, with20–30% of patients facing at least one episode of recurrence even when treated with a therapeutic drug of choice for CDI [21,27]. In a simulated CDI gut model, although vancomycin successfully treated the initial episode of CDI, recurrence occurred approximately18 days after therapy cessation, in which the germination of spores of *C. difficile* in the environment of a biofilm was noted [28]. The recurrence rates of clinical patients with CDI receiving metronidazole and vancomycin therapy, two of the most commonly used anti-*C. difficile* antibiotics, were27.1% and24.0%, respectively [27]. The recurrence could be due to either reinfection of a susceptible individual or reactivation of latent spores within the individual's gastrointestinal tract [27].

CDI recurrence has a multi-factorial complex mechanism, but gut microbiota disruption coincident with viable *C. difficile* spores is considered as the most important factor [28,29]. Of course, targeting spores of *C. difficile* is not the only way to resolve the troublesome CDI recurrence problem; multiple factors, including gut microbiota status and the ribotype of the *C. difficile* (with different spore germination efficiency) also influence the recurrence rate of CDI [26]. For example, rifaximin, though lacking spore-inhibiting effects, can prevent the recurrence of CDI when given immediately after completing standard anti-CDI antibiotics through its relative sparing of enteric microbiota [30–32]. The ribotype of *C. difficile* with different spore germination efficiencies will influence the recurrent rate of CDI; for example, ribotype027 isolates exhibit significantly higher germination efficiencies in the presence of sodium taurocholate than ribotype106 and ribotype078 [26].

Even with the influence of the gut microbiota condition and the ribotype of CDI, developing antimicrobial agents with both anti-*C. difficile* and spore-inhibiting effects have been proven to provide a way to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence, including fidaxomicin, one of the drugs of choice for CDI, and cadazolid and ridinilazole, two antimicrobial agents still in phase II clinical trials (Table1) [33–37].

## The application of the spore-inhibiting effect of current anti-*C. difficile* antimicrobial agents in the therapy of *C. difficile* infection and its recurrenceThe effectiveness of an anti-*C. difficile* antimicrobial agent toward CDI cannot guarantee its inhibitory effect on spores of *C. difficile* and vice versa [38–40]. Though many antimicrobial agents are regarded as drugs of choice for CDI, such as fidaxomicin and vancomycin, their inhibitory effects on *C. difficile* spores are diverse, which might be due to their different adherent and inhibitory effects toward spores of *C. difficile* [38,39]; in contrast, tigecycline and piperacillin/tazobactam, two commonly used antimicrobial agents in the clinic, both have a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on spore production at subminimum inhibitory concentrations (sub-MICs) in-vitro, but their clinical application is limited because of their inadequate therapeutic effect on CDI [16,40,41]. If an antimicrobial agent, such as fidaxomicin, has both anti-vegetative cell and anti-spore effects toward *C. difficile*, it is assumed to be able to not only achieve a therapeutic effect but also lower the recurrence rate [33]. In contrast, if an antimicrobial agent, such as vancomycin, has only anti-vegetative cell effects but lacks anti-spore effects toward *C. difficile*, it will be hypothetically only achieving a therapeutic effect but with a possible high recurrence rate after therapy unless there is some modification of the antimicrobial agents to strengthen its effect on spores [38,39].

Fidaxomicin, a drug used for CDI therapy, can inhibit both the sporulation and the outgrowth of a vegetative cell from the germinating spore, but its effect on the germination of *C. difficile* spores is limited (Table1) [30,42–45]. Fidaxomicin has a persistent inhibitory effect on sporulation when added to early-stationary-phase cells in *C. difficile* strains, including the epidemic NAP1/BI/027 strain at sub-MICs, and thus prevents subsequent growth and toxin production in-vitro; in contrast, vancomycin and metronidazole do not inhibit sporulation at similar sub-MICs [30,43,44]. In contrast to its inhibitory effect on sporulation, fidaxomicin was found to have no inhibitory effect on the initiation of *C. difficile* spore germination by analyzing the kinetics of the initiation of spore germination [42].

The spore-inhibiting effect of fidaxomicin has been illustrated in clinical trials, although the clinical cure rates with fidaxomicin were similar to those with vancomycin in both the modified intention-to-treat analysis (88.2% with fidaxomicin and85.8% with vancomycin) and per-protocol analysis (92.1% and89.8%, respectively), significantly fewer patients in the fidaxomicin group than in the vancomycin group had a recurrence of the infection, in both the modified intention-to-treat analysis (15.4% vs.25.3%, P=0.005) and per-protocol analysis (13.3% vs.24.0%, P=0.004) [46]. The lower recurrence rate following fidaxomicin therapy compared to vancomycin was also due to its lower effect on the microbiota [15,47–50]. In the mice model, fidaxomicin reduced the proportion of Clostridial growth to a lesser extent, but increased that of Bacteroidia, resulting in less disturbance in microbiota diversity [47]. The lesser influence on the microbiota composition of fidaxomicin, compared to vancomycin, promoted faster microbial recovery in the gut, and had more colonization resistance to *C. difficile* [48–50].

Prolonged adherence to the exosporium has been proposed as a possible way of inhibiting spores; as a result, redesigning anti-*C. difficile* antimicrobial agents with the ability to adhere to the exosporium may provide another pathway for the development of anti-*C. difficile* spore agents [38,39]. Vancomycin, although considered as one of the drugs of choice for CDI, was found to have no inhibitory effect on the initiation of *C. difficile* spore germination by analyzing the kinetics of the initiation of spore germination [42]. Thus, the recurrence rate after vancomycin therapy was as high as24.0% [27]. Although vancomycin itself has no effect on *C. difficile* spores, a vancomycin-loaded spore-targeting iron oxide nanoparticle (van-IONP) that selectively binds to *C. difficile* spores has been developed to successfully delay spore germination [38].

## Potential future armament for inhibiting *C. difficile* spores and preventing recurrence of *C. difficile* infectionSome antimicrobial agents undergoing clinical trials have shown excellent anti-*C. difficile* and spore-inhibiting effects, which can not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence (Table1) [33–37].

Cadazolid, a novel fluoroquinolone-oxazolidinone antibiotic in phase II and III trials currently, exhibits potent in-vitro activity against *C. difficile* and its spores [33,34], and has limited effect on the gut microflora, including the *B. fragilis* group and *Lactobacillus* spp. [51,52]. The cure rates of patients with CDI that received250,500, or1000 mg cadazolid twice daily were76.5%,80.0%,68.4%, respectively, compared to68.2% in the group treated with125 mg vancomycin four times daily; in addition, each dosage of cadazolid resulted in a lower recurrence rate than vancomycin (18.2–25.0% vs.50%, respectively) [33]. It is a pity in phase III study cadazolid did not achieve its primary endpoint of non-inferiority to vancomycin for clinical cure in one of two phase III *C. difficile* infection trials [51]. Nevertheless pooling the data from two studies with three randomized controlled trials, cadazolid revealed no significantly difference in sustained clinical response at clinical follow-up (pooled odds ratio (OR)=1.14; P=0.27) but lower recurrence rate (pooled OR=0.71; P=0.04) compared to vancomycin [53].

Ridinilazole, a novel class of heterocyclic antibacterial drugs, can inhibit DNA bacterial synthesis and thus inhibit the growth of *C. difficile* [36,53]. Treatment with supra-MIC concentrations (4× and40× MIC) of ridinilazole resulted in a significant reduction in vegetative cells over72 h (4 log difference, P<0.01) compared with controls without inducing spore formation [36,54]. Ridinilazole, compared to vancomycin, had almost no effect on the gut microbiota, including several Bacteroidaceae and Clostridiaceae families, and maintained the intestinal bile acid profile [35,55]. In phase II trials, the sustained clinical response in patients in the ridinilazole group was66.7%, which was superior to that of42.4% in the vancomycin group [35]. Of note, the recurrence rate of CDI among patients receiving ridinilazole was14.3%, which was lower than that of34.8% for vancomycin [35].

Ramoplanin, a glycolipodepsipeptide antibiotic that is active against *C. difficile*, results in spore counts consistently below the level of detection for28 days after even a brief (30-min) exposure in-vitro [39]. In the same study investigating exposure to ramoplanin, an increase in spore counts was noted after removal of the *C. difficile* exosporium, which suggests that rather than being directly sporicidal, ramoplanin adheres to the exosporium for a prolonged period, and during this time it is available to attack the germinating cells [39]. In hamster models of CDI, *C. difficile* spores were recovered significantly more often from the cecal contents of vancomycin-treated hamsters (n=19/23) compared with ramoplanin-treated (n=6/23) hamsters (P<0.05) [37]. It is unfortunate that though ramoplanin revealed inhibitory effects on *C. difficile* and its spores in-vitro, its clinical efficacy toward CDI and its recurrence is still lacking [32].

CRS3123, a fully synthetic diaryldiamine antimicrobial drug, prevents both *C. difficile* growth and spore production by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, with a >10-fold reduction in the sporulation rate in-vitro [56]. To date, only data from a phase I study assessing the safety and tolerability of CRS3123 are available, and evidence of its clinical effect on CDI and its recurrence is deficient [32].

Nisin, a bacteriocin produced by several strains of *Lactococcus lactis*, was noted to have inhibitory activity against clinical isolates of *C. difficile*, with spore viability reduced by40–50% in-vitro [57]. However, in-vivo evidence of nisin in treating CDI or its recurrence is absent.

Development of a vaccine targeting the spores of *C. difficile* provides a feasible pathway for preventing CDI recurrence [58]. Anti-spore IgY from chickens delayed the occurrence of diarrhea by1.5 d and the spore adherence to the colonic mucosa by90% in a mouse model, and co-administration of anti-spore IgY coupled with vancomycin delayed the appearance of recurrent diarrhea by a median of2 days [58].

Some small molecules and compounds were noted to have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but a determination of their "real" clinical efficacy needs further clinical trials [59,60]. Carvacrol, a food-grade, plant-derived compound, significantly reduces sporulation, germination and spore outgrowth of *C. difficile* and downregulates critical genes involved in spore production in-vitro [59]. Rhodomyrtone, a bioactive compound derived from the leaves of the rose myrtle (*Rhodomyrtus tomentosa*), is four-fold more potent than vancomycin in inhibiting *C. difficile* spore outgrowth in-vitro [60].

## ConclusionDeveloping an antimicrobial agent with a good inhibitory effect on both *C. difficile* vegetative cells and spores can be expected to not only treat CDI but also prevent its recurrence, such as fidaxomicin. Cadazolid and ridinilazole possess a spore-inhibiting effect in-vitro, and thus decrease the recurrence of CDI after cessation of the drug in phase II and III clinical trials. Some small molecules and compounds were noted to have spore-inhibiting effects in-vitro, but the determination of their "real" clinical efficacy requires further clinical trials.

Another iron inC. difﬁciles re
Hal Drakesmith
1,
*
and Michael B. Zimmermann
1
1
MRC Translational Immune Discovery Unit, MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine, Radcliffe Department of Medicine, University
of Oxford, Oxford OX3 0EU, UK
*Correspondence:alexander.drakesmith@imm.ox.ac.uk

Iron is arguably the most important nutrient in the ongoing battle between hosts and bacteria. Recently in
Nature, a unique iron storage organelle, the ferrosome, was discovered in the human pathogenClostridioides
difﬁcile.
1
But what is the role of ferrosomes and how do they affect bacterial behavior and infection?
In 1925, Otto Warburg asserted, Every
living cell contains iron and that life
without iron is impossible.
2
Iron holds
a distinctive position in biochemistry
because of its ability to shuttle electrons
and form bonds with a diverse range of
protein partners. Consequently, iron is a
key co-factor for many enzyme systems
conserved across kingdoms of life. Iron
is a crucial metal resource scavenged by
invading bacteria from infected mamma-
lian hosts. The concept of nutritional im-
munity, where hosts protect their iron re-
sources, but pathogen adaptation can
overcome such defenses, is a well-estab-
lished theme in evolutionary genetics with
some beautiful examples.
3,4
A further
consideration is that because of its chem-
ical reactivity, too much iron is perilous for
a cell. Therefore, microbes must be able
to both efciently acquire iron from a usu-
ally ungenerous host and yet defend
themselves against toxic overabundance.
Adding to this complexity, signicant
changes in iron concentration may occur
in the intestinal lumen. This can happen,
for instance, when iron from food remains
unabsorbed or in cases of gastrointestinal
inammation and/or bleeding.
Clostridioides difﬁcileis a gram-positive
anaerobic bacillus rst described in 1935
in the stool of healthy newborns.
C. difﬁcileinfection (CDI) was thought to
be nonpathogenic until it was identied
as the source of exotoxins in stools of pa-
tients with pseudomembranous colitis.
There has been a sharp increase in CDI
incidence and mortality across industrial-
ized countries and it is now the most
frequently reported nosocomial pathogen
in the United States.
5
CDI may complicate
the course of inammatory bowel disease
(IBD) and cause serious exacerbations of
their disease with high recurrence rates.
6
Prevention and treatment options of
CDI are limited and new strategies for
treating this major public health threat
are needed. Thus, the report by Pi et al.
1
is of importance because a better basic
understanding of CDI could lead to new
therapeutic options. Because replication
ofC. difﬁcileis facilitated by iron acquisi-
tion, an iron-oriented study ofClostri-
dioidesbiology was warranted.
In the search to understand how
C. difﬁcilemaintains iron homeostasis, Pi
et al. revealed the presence of ferrosomes
in these bacteria. Ferrosomes are mem-
brane-bound organelles containing iron,
phosphorous, and oxygen originally iden-
tied inDesulfovibrio magneticusRS-1.
The term was coined when their presence
was also noted inRhodopseudomonas
palustrisandShewanella putrefaciens
and shown to be encoded by the rather
broadly phylogenetically distributedfez
operon.
7
InS. putrefaciens,ferrosomes
likely enable anaerobic adaptation to
iron starvation.
7
However, their function
inC. difﬁcileappears to be more nuanced.
Thefezoperon inC. difﬁcilecontains
two transcription start sites and protein-
coding genesfezAandfezB, the latter of
which shares >30% sequence identity
with P1B6-ATPase transporter that medi-
ates ferrosome formation in gram-nega-
tive anaerobes. Pi et al. investigated the
regulation and function offezB.Thefez
operon was strongly induced by both
iron deprivation and knockout of the tran-
scription factorfur, which is active when
cells are iron replete. However,fezBdele-
tion did not confer a growth defect under
conditions of iron deprivation or iron
excess. Instead, a lag in growth was
observed whenfezB-decient, iron-
deprived cells were exposed to a strong
dose of iron sulfate. Pi et al. suggest thefezsystem may be induced in order to
protect an iron decient cell from a sud-
den inux of potentially toxic iron.
Using a combination of scanning trans-
mission electron microscopy, energy
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, electron
tomography, LC-MS-MS, and cryo-elec-
tron tomography,C. difﬁcilewere then
rigorously analyzed for ferrosome-type
structures. The authors showed that the
fezoperon is necessary and sufcient for
formation of Fe, O, and P-containing
membrane-bound amorphous granules
that are associated with FezA and FezB
proteins and are often near the cell
membrane.
Next, the authors tested whether lack of
ferrosomes infezB-decientC. difﬁcile
altered aspects of infection in murine
models. After four days of infection,
mice infected withfezB-decient
C. difﬁcilehad decreased bacterial
burden and exhibited less weight loss
compared with mice infected with wild-
typeC. difﬁcile. In a mouse model of coli-
tis, although weight loss was comparable
between bacterial strains,fezB-decient
C. difﬁciledemonstrated lower coloniza-
tion and less intestinal inammation
compared to WT. Lastly, in the gut, the
iron-sequestering protein calprotectin
was induced by inammation, calprotec-
tin upregulated thefezoperonin vitro
andin vivo, and in mice lacking calprotec-
tin, colonization and weight loss was
unaffected by loss of the ferrosome sys-
tem. These results indicate that ferro-
somes may be needed in mice to coun-
teract a situation of low iron availability
due to nutritional immunity mediated by
calprotectin.
Low iron availability modies many
aspects ofC. difﬁcilebehavior.
8
Pi et al.
suggest ferrosomes facilitateC. difﬁcile

transition from low iron availability to
excess, for example, perhaps in are-
ups of IBD that may involve blood loss.
Besides IBD, another setting in which
pathogens likeC. difÞcilemust adapt to
rapid shifts in colonic iron availability is
in iron-decient young children in low-in-
come countries who are given iron sup-
plements. These supplements produce
large increases in colonic iron because
the absorption of their high iron dose is
low. In controlled intervention studies,
iron supplements given to Kenyan chil-
dren signicantly increased abundances
ofClostridioides, including both
C. difÞcileandC. perfringens.
9
In addition,
antibiotic efcacy against enteropatho-
gens, such asC. difÞcile, may also
be modied by high colonic iron concen-
trations.
10
Other enteropathogens can
thrive in conditions of widely varying iron
supply, and it is possible they also adapt
via ferrosome-like mechanisms. There-
fore, whether ferrosomes contribute to in-
testinal pathology associated with high
doses of oral iron is an intriguing
possibility.
The study by Pi et al. raises further un-
answered questions. Are ferrosomes
more important for detoxifying excess
iron as thein vitroanalysis suggests, or
for protecting against calprotectin-medi-
ated iron deprivation, as the mouse data
indicates, or is it a bit of both? Do ferro-
somes store iron derived from more phys-
iological sources such as heme and die-
tary iron? Does the ferrosome system
only detoxify excess iron or is it alsoused to cope with other environmental
toxic metals? Do different stressors
modulate ferrosome synthesis, so that
some ferrosomes are different from
others? How important are ferrosomes in
humanC. difÞcileinfection? Lastly,
C. difÞcile, like many bacteria, express
the classical iron storage protein,
ferritin. Ferritin, unlikefezoperon tran-
scription, is decreased during iron depri-
vation. How do ferritin and ferrosome syn-
thesis interrelate, and how do cells decide
which iron-storage facility to use?
Overall, the discovery of ferrosomes in
C. difÞcileis an exciting nding that opens
up several lines of investigation in basic
science and antibacterial therapeutics
while providing new insights into how
iron uxes may modulate the intestinal mi-
crobiota in health and disease.

Hal Drakesmith
1,
*
and Michael B. Zimmermann
1
1
MRC Translational Immune Discovery Unit, MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine, Radcliffe Department of Medicine, University
of Oxford, Oxford OX3 0EU, UK
*Correspondence:alexander.drakesmith@imm.ox.ac.uk
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2023.12.008
Iron is arguably the most important nutrient in the ongoing battle between hosts and bacteria. Recently in
Nature, a unique iron storage organelle, the ferrosome, was discovered in the human pathogenClostridioides
difﬁcile.
1
But what is the role of ferrosomes and how do they affect bacterial behavior and infection?
In 1925, Otto Warburg asserted, Every
living cell contains iron and that life
without iron is impossible.
2
Iron holds
a distinctive position in biochemistry
because of its ability to shuttle electrons
and form bonds with a diverse range of
protein partners. Consequently, iron is a
key co-factor for many enzyme systems
conserved across kingdoms of life. Iron
is a crucial metal resource scavenged by
invading bacteria from infected mamma-
lian hosts. The concept of nutritional im-
munity, where hosts protect their iron re-
sources, but pathogen adaptation can
overcome such defenses, is a well-estab-
lished theme in evolutionary genetics with
some beautiful examples.
3,4
A further
consideration is that because of its chem-
ical reactivity, too much iron is perilous for
a cell. Therefore, microbes must be able
to both efciently acquire iron from a usu-
ally ungenerous host and yet defend
themselves against toxic overabundance.
Adding to this complexity, signicant
changes in iron concentration may occur
in the intestinal lumen. This can happen,
for instance, when iron from food remains
unabsorbed or in cases of gastrointestinal
inammation and/or bleeding.
Clostridioides difﬁcileis a gram-positive
anaerobic bacillus rst described in 1935
in the stool of healthy newborns.
C. difﬁcileinfection (CDI) was thought to
be nonpathogenic until it was identied
as the source of exotoxins in stools of pa-
tients with pseudomembranous colitis.
There has been a sharp increase in CDI
incidence and mortality across industrial-
ized countries and it is now the most
frequently reported nosocomial pathogen
in the United States.
5
CDI may complicate
the course of inammatory bowel disease
(IBD) and cause serious exacerbations of
their disease with high recurrence rates.
6
Prevention and treatment options of
CDI are limited and new strategies for
treating this major public health threat
are needed. Thus, the report by Pi et al.
1
is of importance because a better basic
understanding of CDI could lead to new
therapeutic options. Because replication
ofC. difﬁcileis facilitated by iron acquisi-
tion, an iron-oriented study ofClostri-
dioidesbiology was warranted.
In the search to understand how
C. difﬁcilemaintains iron homeostasis, Pi
et al. revealed the presence of ferrosomes
in these bacteria. Ferrosomes are mem-
brane-bound organelles containing iron,
phosphorous, and oxygen originally iden-
tied inDesulfovibrio magneticusRS-1.
The term was coined when their presence
was also noted inRhodopseudomonas
palustrisandShewanella putrefaciens
and shown to be encoded by the rather
broadly phylogenetically distributedfez
operon.
7
InS. putrefaciens,ferrosomes
likely enable anaerobic adaptation to
iron starvation.
7
However, their function
inC. difﬁcileappears to be more nuanced.
Thefezoperon inC. difﬁcilecontains
two transcription start sites and protein-
coding genesfezAandfezB, the latter of
which shares >30% sequence identity
with P1B6-ATPase transporter that medi-
ates ferrosome formation in gram-nega-
tive anaerobes. Pi et al. investigated the
regulation and function offezB.Thefez
operon was strongly induced by both
iron deprivation and knockout of the tran-
scription factorfur, which is active when
cells are iron replete. However,fezBdele-
tion did not confer a growth defect under
conditions of iron deprivation or iron
excess. Instead, a lag in growth was
observed whenfezB-decient, iron-
deprived cells were exposed to a strong
dose of iron sulfate. Pi et al. suggest thefezsystem may be induced in order to
protect an iron decient cell from a sud-
den inux of potentially toxic iron.
Using a combination of scanning trans-
mission electron microscopy, energy
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, electron
tomography, LC-MS-MS, and cryo-elec-
tron tomography,C. difﬁcilewere then
rigorously analyzed for ferrosome-type
structures. The authors showed that the
fezoperon is necessary and sufcient for
formation of Fe, O, and P-containing
membrane-bound amorphous granules
that are associated with FezA and FezB
proteins and are often near the cell
membrane.
Next, the authors tested whether lack of
ferrosomes infezB-decientC. difﬁcile
altered aspects of infection in murine
models. After four days of infection,
mice infected withfezB-decient
C. difﬁcilehad decreased bacterial
burden and exhibited less weight loss
compared with mice infected with wild-
typeC. difﬁcile. In a mouse model of coli-
tis, although weight loss was comparable
between bacterial strains,fezB-decient
C. difﬁciledemonstrated lower coloniza-
tion and less intestinal inammation
compared to WT. Lastly, in the gut, the
iron-sequestering protein calprotectin
was induced by inammation, calprotec-
tin upregulated thefezoperonin vitro
andin vivo, and in mice lacking calprotec-
tin, colonization and weight loss was
unaffected by loss of the ferrosome sys-
tem. These results indicate that ferro-
somes may be needed in mice to coun-
teract a situation of low iron availability
due to nutritional immunity mediated by
calprotectin.
Low iron availability modies many
aspects ofC. difﬁcilebehavior.
8

transition from low iron availability to
excess, for example, perhaps in are-

Besides IBD, another setting in which
pathogens likeC. difÞcilemust adapt to
rapid shifts in colonic iron availability is
in iron-decient young children in low-in-
come countries who are given iron sup-
plements. These supplements produce
large increases in colonic iron because
the absorption of their high iron dose is
low. In controlled intervention studies,
iron supplements given to Kenyan chil-
dren signicantly increased abundances
ofClostridioides, including both
C. difÞcileandC. perfringens.
9
In addition,
antibiotic efcacy against enteropatho-
gens, such asC. difÞcile, may also
be modied by high colonic iron concen-
trations.
10
Other enteropathogens can
thrive in conditions of widely varying iron
supply, and it is possible they also adapt
via ferrosome-like mechanisms. There-
fore, whether ferrosomes contribute to in-
testinal pathology associated with high
doses of oral iron is an intriguing
possibility.
The study by Pi et al. raises further un-
answered questions. Are ferrosomes
more important for detoxifying excess
iron as thein vitroanalysis suggests, or
for protecting against calprotectin-medi-
ated iron deprivation, as the mouse data
indicates, or is it a bit of both? Do ferro-
somes store iron derived from more phys-
iological sources such as heme and die-
tary iron? Does the ferrosome system
only detoxify excess iron or is it alsoused to cope with other environmental
toxic metals? Do different stressors
modulate ferrosome synthesis, so that
some ferrosomes are different from
others? How important are ferrosomes in
humanC. difÞcileinfection? Lastly,
C. difÞcile, like many bacteria, express
the classical iron storage protein,
ferritin. Ferritin, unlikefezoperon tran-
scription, is decreased during iron depri-
vation. How do ferritin and ferrosome syn-
thesis interrelate, and how do cells decide
which iron-storage facility to use?
Overall, the discovery of ferrosomes in
C. difÞcileis an exciting nding that opens
up several lines of investigation in basic
science and antibacterial therapeutics
while providing new insights into how
iron uxes may modulate the intestinal mi-
crobiota in health and disease.

# Another iron in *C. difficile*'s fireHal Drakesmith<sup>1,\*</sup> and Michael B. Zimmermann<sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup> MRC Translational Immune Discovery Unit, MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine, Radcliffe Department of Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford OX30EU, UK\* Correspondence: alexander.drakesmith@imm.ox.ac.ukhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2023.12.008Iron is arguably the most important nutrient in the ongoing battle between hosts and bacteria. Recently in *Nature*, a unique iron storage organelle, the ferrosome, was discovered in the human pathogen *Clostridioides difficile*.<sup>1</sup> But what is the role of ferrosomes and how do they affect bacterial behavior and infection?

In1925, Otto Warburg asserted, "Every living cell contains iron and that life without iron is impossible."<sup>2</sup> Iron holds a distinctive position in biochemistry because of its ability to shuttle electrons and form bonds with a diverse range of protein partners. Consequently, iron is a key co-factor for many enzyme systems conserved across kingdoms of life. Iron is a crucial metal resource scavenged by invading bacteria from infected mammalian hosts. The concept of "nutritional immunity," where hosts protect their iron resources, but pathogen adaptation can overcome such defenses, is a well-established theme in evolutionary genetics with some beautiful examples.<sup>3,4</sup> A further consideration is that because of its chemical reactivity, too much iron is perilous for a cell. Therefore, microbes must be able to both efficiently acquire iron from a usually ungenerous host and yet defend themselves against toxic overabundance. Adding to this complexity, significant changes in iron concentration may occur in the intestinal lumen. This can happen, for instance, when iron from food remains unabsorbed or in cases of gastrointestinal inflammation and/or bleeding.

*Clostridioides difficile* is a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus first described in1935 in the stool of healthy newborns. *C. difficile* infection (CDI) was thought to be nonpathogenic until it was identified as the source of exotoxins in stools of patients with pseudomembranous colitis. There has been a sharp increase in CDI incidence and mortality across industrialized countries and it is now the most frequently reported nosocomial pathogen in the United States.<sup>5</sup> CDI may complicate the course of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and cause serious exacerbations of their disease with high recurrence rates.<sup>6</sup> Prevention and treatment options of CDI are limited and new strategies for treating this major public health threat are needed. Thus, the report by Pi et al.<sup>1</sup> is of importance because a better basic understanding of CDI could lead to new therapeutic options. Because replication of *C. difficile* is facilitated by iron acquisition, an iron-oriented study of *Clostridioides* biology was warranted.

In the search to understand how *C. difficile* maintains iron homeostasis, Pi et al. revealed the presence of ferrosomes in these bacteria. Ferrosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing iron, phosphorous, and oxygen originally identified in *Desulfovibrio magneticus* RS-1. The term was coined when their presence was also noted in *Rhodopseudomonas palustris* and *Shewanella putrefaciens* and shown to be encoded by the rather broadly phylogenetically distributed *fez* operon.<sup>7</sup> In *S. putrefaciens*, ferrosomes likely enable anaerobic adaptation to iron starvation.<sup>7</sup> However, their function in *C. difficile* appears to be more nuanced.

The *fez* operon in *C. difficile* contains two transcription start sites and protein-coding genes *fezA* and *fezB*, the latter of which shares >30% sequence identity with P1B6-ATPase transporter that mediates ferrosome formation in gram-negative anaerobes. Pi et al. investigated the regulation and function of *fezB*. The *fez* operon was strongly induced by both iron deprivation and knockout of the transcription factor *fur*, which is active when cells are iron replete. However, *fezB* deletion did not confer a growth defect under conditions of iron deprivation or iron excess. Instead, a lag in growth was observed when *fezB*-deficient, iron-deprived cells were exposed to a strong dose of iron sulfate. Pi et al. suggest the *fez* system may be induced in order to protect an iron deficient cell from a sudden influx of potentially toxic iron.

Using a combination of scanning transmission electron microscopy, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, electron tomography, LC-MS-MS, and cryo-electron tomography, *C. difficile* were then rigorously analyzed for ferrosome-type structures. The authors showed that the *fez* operon is necessary and sufficient for formation of Fe, O, and P-containing membrane-bound amorphous granules that are associated with FezA and FezB proteins and are often near the cell membrane.

Next, the authors tested whether lack of ferrosomes in *fezB*-deficient *C. difficile* altered aspects of infection in murine models. After four days of infection, mice infected with *fezB*-deficient *C. difficile* had decreased bacterial burden and exhibited less weight loss compared with mice infected with wild-type *C. difficile*. In a mouse model of colitis, although weight loss was comparable between bacterial strains, *fezB*-deficient *C. difficile* demonstrated lower colonization and less intestinal inflammation compared to WT. Lastly, in the gut, the iron-sequestering protein calprotectin was induced by inflammation, calprotectin upregulated the *fez* operon *in vitro* and *in vivo*, and in mice lacking calprotectin, colonization and weight loss was unaffected by loss of the ferrosome system. These results indicate that ferrosomes may be needed in mice to counteract a situation of low iron availability due to nutritional immunity mediated by calprotectin.

Low iron availability modifies many aspects of *C. difficile* behavior.<sup>8</sup> Pi et al. suggest ferrosomes facilitate *C. difficile* transition from low iron availability to excess, for example, perhaps in flare-ups of IBD that may involve blood loss. Besides IBD, another setting in which pathogens like *C. difficile* must adapt to rapid shifts in colonic iron availability is in iron-deficient young children in low-income countries who are given iron supplements. These supplements produce large increases in colonic iron because the absorption of their high iron dose is low. In controlled intervention studies, iron supplements given to Kenyan children significantly increased abundances of *Clostridioides*, including both *C. difficile* and *C. perfringens*.<sup>9</sup> In addition, antibiotic efficacy against enteropathogens, such as *C. difficile*, may also be modified by high colonic iron concentrations.<sup>10</sup> Other enteropathogens can thrive in conditions of widely varying iron supply, and it is possible they also adapt via ferrosome-like mechanisms. Therefore, whether ferrosomes contribute to intestinal pathology associated with high doses of oral iron is an intriguing possibility.

The study by Pi et al. raises further unanswered questions. Are ferrosomes more important for detoxifying excess iron as the *in vitro* analysis suggests, or for protecting against calprotectin-mediated iron deprivation, as the mouse data indicates, or is it a bit of both? Do ferrosomes store iron derived from more physiological sources such as heme and dietary iron? Does the ferrosome system only detoxify excess iron or is it also used to cope with other environmental toxic metals? Do different stressors modulate ferrosome synthesis, so that some ferrosomes are different from others? How important are ferrosomes in human *C. difficile* infection? Lastly, *C. difficile*, like many bacteria, express the "classical" iron storage protein, ferritin. Ferritin, unlike *fez* operon transcription, is decreased during iron deprivation. How do ferritin and ferrosome synthesis interrelate, and how do cells decide which iron-storage facility to use?

Overall, the discovery of ferrosomes in *C. difficile* is an exciting finding that opens up several lines of investigation in basic science and antibacterial therapeutics while providing new insights into how iron fluxes may modulate the intestinal microbiota in health and disease.

ABSTRACTClostridioides difficile previously known as Clostridium difficile is one of the three most potent human pathogens associated with antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and damage to the colon. Although advanced healthcare facilities with the development of new antibiotics are now available, these are associated with either treatment failure or disease recurrence. Any reason that disturbs the microbiome such as antibiotic treatment, unbalanced diet, stress and chronic disease may allow C. difficile, to adhere, colonize, grow and reproduce and eventually cause disease recurrence. With increasing knowledge about the natural defence mechanism of microbiome against gut path-ogens, interest in non-antibiotic alternatives like prebiotics, synbiotics, probiotics, and postbiotics is quickly evolving. The gut microenvironment can be suitably modified by using prebiotics and probiotics either alone or by using their mixture as synbiotics. The gut microbiome prevents pathogen adhesion either by physical competition or by the proliferation of anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial products. Besides, there are other possible methods such as faecal matter transplantation (FMT) and microbiome replacement therapies (MRT) for the repopulation of the gastrointestinal tract. In this article, we review current treatment strategies for C. difficile infection (CDI) using prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, postbiotic FMT, and MRT. The article will give useful insight into the current therapies of CDI and their future developments.
1.Introduction
Clostridioides difficile is an anaerobic and gram-positive bacterium which linked with array of diseases like diarrhoea to fulminant colitis [1]. C. difficile infection (CDI) reduces the biodiversity of the gut biome and causes intestinal dysbiosis. CDI is a major health issue across the globe associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare-associated infection (HAI). C. difficile primarily elicit the disease by the production of two types of toxins such as TcdA and TcdB that upon endocytosis into the colon, inactivate host GTPases, and disrupt the cytoskeleton and neutrophilic influx, which eventually causes cell apoptosis and necrosis [2]. The rigorous healthcare facilities and appropriate antibiotic treatment are the best treatment options for CDI [3,4]. Despite antibiotics being the preliminary treatment strategies for CDI, they are associated with several side effects. Antibiotics like vancomycin or fidaxomicin are significantly used for the treatment of CDI, however, several case relapses have been found after treatment [5,
6]. The indigenous gut microbiome provides resistance against C. difficile colonization; but antibiotic treatment disrupts the micro-biome and increases susceptibility to CDI [7,8]. The symbiotic in-teractions between resident microbes and the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) play a very significant role in gut homeostasis. However, antibiotic abuse, nutritional choices, and other variables are thought to contribute to gut dysbiosis. Therefore, it is prudent to identify alternatives (non--antibiotics) for the treatment of CDI. In a recent study by V´azquez-Cuesta et al., the researchers aimed to investigate the role of the microbiome as a predictive biomarker for CDI. A total of 753 samples from 657 patients were analyzed, including 247 from patients with CDI, 43 from patients colonized with C. difficile, 63 from healthy individuals, 324 from patients without CDI (NOCDI), and 76 from patients with recurrent CDI (R-CDI). The study revealed significant differences in both alpha and beta diversity, as well as in taxonomic abundance across these groups. Prebiotics are particularly utilized by the host for their health- giving, while probiotics comprise live bacterium that can be beneficial for their health when given in correct doses. Whereas synbiotics are a mixture of probiotics and prebiotics which are good for human health. Through microbial population shifts in the gut, synbiotics start making short-chain fatty acids, which can promote defence against infections, reduce inflammation, increase satiety, and improve bowel function [10,11]. In this article, different strategies of protection against CDI used in present scenarios such as prebiotics, synbiotics, probiotics, FMT, and MBT and their prospects will be discussed in detail.
2.Gut microbiome and their role in human health
The gut microbiome plays crucial role to manage the body’s in-flammatory response, metabolic processes, immunological activity, and even neurological functions [12,13]. It produces vitamins, hormones, and neurotransmitters and causes the breakdown of the dietary com-ponents. The gut microbiome can also influence the host’s metabolic pathways such as absorption and metabolism of nutrients, and synthesis of metabolites. The gut of human beings compasses diverse group of microorganisms such as archaea, bacteria, fungi, and viruses are pre-sent. These microorganisms are responsible for maintaining gut health, by regulating digestion, metabolism, and protection against infections (Fig. 1). The composition of the microbiome is influenced by numerous aspects such as diet, age, and health status. Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes are the prevalent bacterial group present in the gut, whereas Actino-bacteria, Verrucomicrobia, and Proteobacteria are also frequent [14,15]. The most common species of microbiota reported in the gut are Bifidobacterium spp., Bacteroides spp., Clostridium spp., Enterobacter spp., 
Enterococcus spp., Gemella spp., Megasphaera spp., Porphyromonas spp., Pseudomonas spp., Prevotella spp., Rothia spp., Ruminococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Veillonella spp [16]. These microorganisms are usu-ally commensal or mutualists and they primarily aid in regulating metabolism, such as glucose fermentation which produces butyrate, as a bioproduct that works as an essential form of energy for colonocytes. Intestinal microbes also beneficially influence lipid metabolism. They improve protein metabolism by using microbial proteinases and pepti-dases. They are also necessary to produce different vitamins such as vitamin B12, vitamin K, biotin, conjugated linoleic acids etc. They are involved in the degradation of different polyphenols and convert bile acids [17].Many bacteria that are associated with the daily aspects of life can be found in the digestive tract of a healthy individual [18]. The ecology and function of gut bacteria are dynamic in infancy, but they stabilize throughout childhood [19]. These acquired new gut microbiota influ-ence the digestion and the immunologic responses of the host [20,21]. The gut microbiota changes gradually with age in response to devel-oping immune systems [22]. Different environmental factors can also disturb the gut microbiota and are a key indicator of long-term health. The intestinal microbiome not only affects the gut rather it influences every organ of the body via a variety of mechanisms [23]. The external variables can modify the intestinal biome, which offers novel treatment options for some ailments [24]. A healthy gut is necessary for energy harvesting and proper body functions. Besides gut microbiome also af-fects metabolic health, such as blood glucose level, blood pressure, and atherosclerosis, neurological problems, behavioural and inflammatory responses [25]. Recently, the gut microbiome has been considered for its promising characteristic in epilepsy [26].

Supplementing with probiotics e.g., Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium may assist to maintain the balance of microbes in the gut and decrease the chances of the recurrence of CDIs [52,53]. Probiotics can also boost immunity, and thereby guide the body to block the pathogens. Pro-biotics reduce oxidative stress associated with inflammatory diseases.Several findings support probiotics inhibiting pathogen growth and toxicity (Table 1). The use of probiotics to stop the growth of C. difficile has been assessed using various techniques [54,55]. Several studies show that a few species of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can reduce C. difficile’s adherence to the epithelial cell line and mucus of the in-testine [56,57]. Although there is little evidence on the potential effectiveness of probiotics in CDI treatment, most clinical investigations to date have concentrated on prevention. There are some cases where probiotic combination together with any antibiotic prescriptions under C. difficile outbreak, decreased the number of C. difficile cases [58] (Table 1). According to meta-analysis studies, probiotics have continu-ously demonstrated a positive function, in preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD) in children [59,60]. Recently, Lukasik et al. found a multispecies probiotic’s effectiveness in prevent-ing AAD in children [61]. Therefore, using appropriate probiotic composition in children receiving antibiotic treatment could be a pos-sibility to reduce diarrhoea.Meta-analysis has revealed the prospective of two bacterium L. rhamnosus. and S. boulardii in the CDI treatment. Bifidobacteria su-pernatants isolated from the gut of physically fit infants inhibited the growth and adhesion of C. difficile to enterocytes [62]. Whereas the consumption of B. bifidum modulated the gut environment in healthy adults [63]. The mixture of different Lactobacillus species has been found effective in many clinical trials. A probiotic capsule containing four-strain of Lactobacillus improved diarrhoea in CDI patients [64]. The intake of L. acidophilus, L. casei, and L. rhamnosus combination dimin-ished the CDI up to 2.3 cases per ten thousand patients [65]. Similarly, the CDI incidence among immunocompromised patients has been reduced from 1.21 % to 0.11 % using L. plantarum [66]. Adjunct pro-biotics containing L. bulgaricus, L. casei, and S. thermophiles prevented the CDI risk by up to 17 % in patients receiving antibiotic treatment 
[67]. These clinical trial findings emphasize the role of Lactobacillus species as a nontoxic and effective probiotic in CDI prevention and their recurrence. S. boulardii can also significantly help in restoring the antibiotic-disrupted microbiome [68]. S. boulardii CNCM I-745 pro-hibited the consequences and recurrence of CDIs in the hamster model [69–71] (Table 1).Besides the above species, some species of Bacteroides and Clostridium are also used as prebiotic agents for the CDI treatment. B. fragilis strain ZY-312 increased the beneficial microbe of the gut Akkermansia muci-niphila, which prevents C. difficile colonization in the gut [72]. Similarly, B. thetaiotaomicron increased the population of useful bacteria Bacter-oidetes, Proteobacteria and Verruco microbiota and suppressed the C. difficile in the gut [73]. Nonetheless, more clinical trials are essential to confirm the effectiveness of Bacteroides as some of their genera have been found invading the gut microbiome [72,73]. The probiotic mixture containing Bacillus mesentericus, C. butyricum, and S. faecalis, prevented CDIs in elderly patients undergoing femoral fracture surgery (Nagamine, Matsumoto et al., 2019). However, there is no therapeutic usefulness of C. butyricum in adjuvant therapy. In recent times, the probiotic combi-nation containing S. boulardii, or C. butyricum and Lactobacillus species has been widely used for CDI prophylaxis (Nagamine, Matsumoto et al., 2019).Sometimes antibiotics have toxic effects on probiotics while sup-plementation. An appealing solution to the antibiotics’ lethal activity on probiotics may be the physical encapsulation of the latter in a protective shell (Fig. 3). Currently, various polymeric particles have been devel-oped to promote the colonization and presence of probiotics in the GIT, but an efficient, safe, and quick coating with broad-spectrum antibiotic resistance is yet to be developed [74]. The use of natural polyphenols to create a nano armour coating for bacteria in the GIT is a novel approach to protect bacteria from antibiotics [74]. This coating could act as a barrier, allowing bacteria to survive the presence of antibiotics in the GIT. Natural polyphenols, such as those derived from fruits, vegetables, and nuts, have antimicrobial properties that may help to protect bacteria from antibiotics. Additionally, the polyphenol coating could help to reduce the number of antibiotics that are taken up by the bacteria, thus

gastrointestinal microbiome, engineered probiotics could be used to retain the balance [75]. These probiotics are specifically designed to target C. difficile and reduce its presence in the intestines [76]. They can also promote the re-establishment of good bacteria like Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus species in the gut, which can further improve digestive health and decrease the risk of infection. Besides restoring the gut microbiome balance, engineered probiotics can also help to lessen the inflammatory reaction and improve the overall health of the digestive system [77].Advancements in gene editing technology have opened new oppor-tunities for probiotic application in CDI treatment. Researchers have been able to use gene editing techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 to modify the genes of certain probiotic strains to improve their efficacy and safety [78]. CRISPR/Cas9 technique can modify the genes of certain probiotic strains to increase their resistance to antibiotics and other drugs, improve their digestive health benefits, and enhance their ability to produce beneficial substances [79]. Additionally, gene editing tech-niques have been used to add new genes to probiotic strains, allowing them to produce compounds with therapeutic benefits, such as anti-inflammatory or anti-cancer agents. Finally, gene editing tech-niques have been used to delete genes from probiotic strains, allowing them to produce fewer harmful substances. Overall, gene editing tech-nology provides a powerful tool to engineer probiotic strains that are more effective and safer for human consumption. By now, several modified probiotics have progressed to the clinical trial stage. The latest advancement in the field of gene editing is CRISPR-Cas9 technology. This technology enables precise editing of any gene sequence by combining DNA-cutting enzymes and RNA-guided proteins. By altering gene sequences, researchers can develop new probiotics with desirable traits [80].Another advancement in the field is the development of gene-editing tools that target specific cells within the probiotic [81]. These tools are used to modify the genetic makeup of the probiotic, which improves the performance of the probiotic or to create new strains with improved stability in the GIT, and increased tolerance to antibiotics. Additionally, gene-editing tools have been used to engineer probiotic bacteria with the ability to produce therapeutic proteins that can help reduce inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity, and fight off infections [78].Gene editing technology is advancing rapidly and is likely to revo-lutionize the world of probiotics. This technology has the potential to revolutionize the way people can improve their health, with potential applications ranging from targeted treatments for diseases to improving the performance of probiotic supplements. With gene editing, scientists can modify the genetic code of microorganisms, allowing for the crea-tion of new probiotic strains with tailored benefits to individual needs. The possibilities for gene editing in the field of probiotics are virtually limitless and could ultimately result in improved health outcomes for people around the world. For example, gene editing could be used to engineer probiotics that are better able to survive in the gut, thereby boosting their effectiveness. It could also be used to create probiotics that are designed to target specific diseases or conditions, allowing for a more personalized approach to health [82]. Additionally, gene editing techniques could allow the development of probiotics that are person-alized to individual dietary requirements, having greater precision and effectiveness. As technology continues to evolve, it is believable to have substantial impact on probiotics research, revolutionizing how they are used for health benefits. Engineered microbes with inflammatory bowel disease applications have also been developed by scientists [83].
5.3.Prebiotic approaches
Earlier the prebiotics definition was limited to the non-digestible food item which significantly benefited the host but later, it was broadened to encompass both carbohydrates (e.g., Fructo- oligosaccharides (FOS), inulin, lactulose, galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS)) and dietary prebiotics. Dietary prebiotics are described as “the 
ingredients that positively affect the composition and/or activity of the gut microbiome for the health profit of the host” [84]. However, the most important aspect of prebiotics is their association with human well-being, as their beneficial effects are further enhanced through cross-feeding [85].Prebiotics can help to renew the overall healthy balance of microbes in the gut as well as reduce the risk of recurrence of C. difficile infections [86]. They must meet criteria such as resistance to acidic pH, non-hydrolysable by host enzymes, non-absorbable in the GIT, and fermentable by intestinal microorganisms [87]. For carbohydrate-derived prebiotics the degree of polymerization must be ≥3 [88].There are several types of prebiotics such as glucose-derived oligo-saccharides, galacto-oligosaccharides, pectic oligosaccharides, fructans, starch, and other oligosaccharides carbohydrates (OSCs) which are very useful in mitigating CDIs (Table 2). Naturally different dietary food products like pulses and vegetables are rich sources of prebiotics but recently, prebiotics have been obtained from seaweed and microalgae as well [89]. However, due to its lower concentration in foods, nowadays industries are producing it at large scales.Over the past few years there has been an increased role of poly-phenols as prebiotic agents.
