encompasses the transfer of faecal matter from a physically fit person’s stool to a recipient that helps to repair the gut microbiome and treat conditions like inflammatory bowel and antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (Fig. 4). FMT is the utmost effective form of MRT for recurrent CDI cases, with a recovery rate of over 90 %. FMT has been used for over 1700 years in traditional systems of medicine to treat a variety of illnesses [110]. Recent research has revealed that healthy commensal bacteria in the gut can collaborate to produce beneficial metabolites with anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and even antifungal properties. These metabolites might be accountable for the health-promoting effects of FMT. In addition, FMT also modulates the immune response, reduces inflammation, and restores a balanced gut microbiota. Kamierczak-Siedlecka et al. studied the molecular mechanisms of FMT and found that several bacterial species are important for the successful outcome of FMT, including Bacteroides fragilis, Roseburia intestinalis, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii [111].FMT is a rapidly developing therapeutic approach that has become a focus of biomedical and clinical studies. It is used as a last resort when other therapies for C. difficile have failed. FMT is specifically composed of well-known probiotic microbes that have been selected for their ability to provide health benefits through one or more mechanisms. In clinical studies, fecal matter transfer is generally safe and effective in treating CDI with a success rate of over 90 % and few adverse effects reported [112]. As research continues, the potential benefits of faecal matter transfer may become clearer. However, further clinical trials are essential to establish the efficacy of FMT in CDI [111].Before samples can be accepted, donors must be meticulously tested and vetted. To preserve the bacteria, the stool samples are diluted in saline and filtered, and then glycerol is added. This sample is then stored at 80 
◦C. The sample is administered in liquid form to the transplant recipient. It can be transported either through the anus into the large intestine using a colonoscopy, or via the nose and into the small intestine using a nasoduodenal tube (NGT). Additionally, the donor’s stool sam-ple is tested for any dangerous bacteria, viruses, and parasites. FMT helps to restore a healthy bacterial balance in the colon. FMT is usually performed with a colonoscopy, however, it can also be performed with a less common approach, such as an NGT. During a colonoscopy, the co-lonoscope is inserted into the colon and moved through the total length of the colon. As the colonoscope is removed, the stool is delivered into the colon. The stool contains healthy bacteria and other microbial or-ganisms that help to restore a healthy bacterial balance in the colon. Additionally, FMT can help to reduce symptoms related to the bowels, Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis, and CDI.Faecal transplantation via colonoscopy was found very suitable in the treatment of recurrent CDI, which can recur in up to 50 % of patients receiving antibiotics [113]. The potential role of FMT to treat CDI has created a new area of research into microbiome-based restorative therapies.A pooled analysis of recurrent CDI cases by FMT via colonoscopy or nasogastric tube (NGT) has been conducted by Postigo and Kim, to determine the efficacy of the procedure. The results indicated that FMT by colonoscopy or NGT could be an effective solution for the recurrent CDI, regardless of procedure alterations. However, further studies are required to explore the optimal delivery route for FMT [114,115].The latest report of the treatment of a 78-year-old man suffering from Pseudomembranous Colitis due to C. difficile persistence in the stool sample from New Delhi, India. FMT by a healthy person’s stool helped to cure these severe cases (Link20.01.22).There are some unsuccessful cases of FMT as well. For example, In Italy while treating CDI with FMT (colonoscopy) only 69 % of patients recovered by a single faecal dose, whereas the remaining 31 % required repeat infusions [116]. The recovery rate of patients suffering from CDI varied from 14 % to 59 % in the United States due to application of non-specific antibiotics, severe and fulminant CDI, and pseudomem-branous colitis. Moreover, FMT was associated with numerous side ef-fects such as abdominal cramping, bloating, diarrhoea, and nausea 
[117]. Besides two patients receiving FMT from the same donor suffered from bacteriemia caused by E. coli, and one patient died [118]. Thus, the selection of suitable donors and recipients is very crucial for performing FMT.
5.7.Treatment of C. difficile by targeting toxins A (TcdA) and B (TcdB)
There are various antibiotics such as metronidazole or vancomycin available for CDI treatment. These antibiotics mainly inhibit the toxins (TcdA and TcdB) secreted by C. difficile, thus preventing further colon damage. Additionally, probiotics may be utilized to reinstate the balance of microbes in the gut. Treatment of C. difficile typically involves the use of antibiotics to decrease the bacterial counts. However, in some cases, antibiotics may not be enough to eradicate the infection. In these cases, targeting the toxins produced by C. difficile may reduce the severity of the infection. TcdA and TcdB are two of the most potent toxins produced by C. difficile. To target these toxins, several medications have been developed. These medications can include antibody-based therapies or small molecule inhibitors that prevent toxin production or neutralize its activity. In some cases, a combination of antibiotics and other treat-ments may be necessary to successfully treat C. difficile.Scientists have recently proposed that serine proteases from two probiotic strains, Saccharomyces boulardii and Bacillus clausii, could be used to prevent CDI. A serine protease from S. boulardii has been shown to disrupt the quorum sensing mechanism of C. difficile, an important regulatory mechanism. Moreover, this protease was also shown to effectively suppress the toxin TcdA. Similarly, a protease from B. clausii was found to be effective against TcdB. Both proteases have demon-strated efficacy in vivo and in vitro, suggesting that they may be prom-ising targets for further research regarding the prevention of CDI [119]. The toxins TcdA and TcdB required for C. difficile-caused diarrhoea are produced by pathogenic strains. An alternate treatment fare CDI that has revealed encouraging outcomes in preclinical and clinical investigations is the administration of anti-toxin antibodies [120].In a recent study, Hunag and McCreary reported that Clostridium butyricum is useful in treating a variety of gastrointestinal conditions. C. difficile was reported to be significantly inhibited by supernatants of the C. butyricum MIYAIRI 588 strain (CBM588). A proteinaceous component may be important in preventing C. difficile growth in vitro, according to features of the supernatant from CBM 588 that are heat- and pH-labile [121]. It has been established that recombinant CBM 588 bacteriocin (CBM-B) has an inhibitory effect against C. difficile, however, spore germination and outgrowth were unaffected. By lowering the expression of a toxin regulator when used at sub-lethal concentrations, CBM-B could partially suppress the expression of toxins (tcdA and tcdB). A mice infected with CDI, intra-rectal injection of CBM-B in combination with vancomycin lead to in less body weight loss and a lower C. difficile bacterial count in faeces than did CBM-B or vancomycin administration alone. As a result, CBM-B from CBM 588 has the potential to be an in-hibitor of C. difficile and a possible therapeutic therapy for CDI.The effectiveness of human monoclonal antibodies (HuMab) and polyclonal antibodies against C. difficile toxins TcdA and TcdB were examined in a genotobiotic piglet model of CDI by Steele et al. [122,123] The results showed that TcdB was a major virulence factor contributing to both systemic and gastrointestinal (GI) tract diseases. Administration of anti-TcdB antibodies alone or in combination with anti-TcdA completely prevented systemic CDI in piglets and significantly reduced GI lesions. In contrast, pigs who received only anti-TcdA experienced severe GI and systemic illnesses with a 67–83 % death rate, performing worse than the control animals which had been given a placebo [123].
5.8.Postbiotic approach against CDI
The concept of postbiotics, which emerged in 2021, is currently being widely studied [124]. Postbiotics are a form of metabolic 
C. Singh et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Medicine in Microecology 24 (2025) 100121 9 

byproducts or non-viable bacterial products produced by probiotic mi-croorganisms, which exert a biological effect on the host. Postbiotics are composed of functional bioactive compounds created in an anaerobic matrix, resulting from the fermentation of prebiotics and other organic nutrients which generate energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate. These byproducts, often of low molecular weight, include short-chain fatty acids, microbial cell fragments, extracellular polysaccharides, cell lysates, teichoic acid, vitamins, and more [125]. While prebiotics and probiotics are currently the most popular products on the market, postbiotics are gaining an increasing amount of attention due to their numerous health benefits (Fig. 5). Probiotics are increasingly recognized as a valuable tool for restoring balance to the intestinal microbiota disrupted by factors such as antibiotic therapy. This disruption can create an environment conducive to the overgrowth of C. difficile, leading to a rise in C. difficile-associated infections. Although many probiotics have demonstrated in vitro efficacy in inhibiting the growth or toxicity of C. difficile, their use in treating or preventing CDI remains limited due to a lack of robust clinical evidence. Only a few strains, notably Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii, have been extensively studied. The growing understanding of how probiotics combat C. difficile through various mechanisms reviewed here suggests that these live biotherapeutic agents hold promise for CDI management. However, there is a need for more rigorous and standardized clinical studies to evaluate probiotic products in conjunction with antibiotics, to identify the most effective candidates for preventing or treating C. difficile infections [55]. Given these insights, it is likely that the de-mand for postbiotic supplements will rise in the future. Postbiotics, known for their antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodu-latory properties, are emerging as a promising option for treating or preventing CDI. Research has demonstrated that postbiotics can inhibit the growth of Clostridium difficile in both in vitro studies and animal models, as well as reduce toxin production. Furthermore, postbiotic therapy appears beneficial for premature infants, who frequently lack beneficial bacteria. This therapy has been shown to mitigate inflam-mation, improve digestion, and enhance overall health in these vulnerable patients [121,126].Postbiotics can be administered via food, supplements, or enemas. These beneficial compounds are believed to offer a range of protective effects, such as producing substances that reduce inflammation, bolster the body’s natural defenses, and support healthy intestinal tissue. Evi-dence suggests that postbiotic therapy is both safe and effective in managing various intestinal disorders in premature infants [127].
In a recent study, Luenglusontigit et al. first used a high-throughput screening approach to isolate and identify E. faecalis strains that pro-duced bacteriocin-like compounds [128]. Screening of bacteriocin pro-duction of E. faecalis PK1201 was achieved through proteolytic enzyme treatment, followed by whole genome sequencing to characterize bacteriocin-encoding genes. A postbiotic of E. faecalis PK1201 was then prepared using neutralized cell-free supernatant or bacterial cell lysate, which was screened for antimicrobial activity using agar well diffusion. The lyophilized cell-free supernatant (LCFS) was subsequently tested for its minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against C. difficile 630. Morphological changes of C. difficile were observed under scanning electron microscopes. The LCFS at both sub-MIC and MIC concentrations were used to evaluate anti-spore germination activity. Finally, the safety of the postbiotic was evaluated using the Galleria mellonella model. The efficacy and safety of LCFS has illuminated the role of postbiotics in pharmaceutical products for the control of CDI [128].Postbiotics have demonstrated the ability to support gut microbiota health and reduce inflammation, which may help lower the risk of CDI. They may also be effective in treating recurrent CDI by restoring gut microbiota balance. In addition, postbiotics show great promise as an adjunctive treatment for CDI due to their capacity to inhibit bacterial growth, disrupt biofilms, and reduce toxin production, offering a po-tential solution to antibiotic-resistant pathogens [129]. However, further research is needed to confirm the efficacy and safety of these compounds in treating CDI.
6.Conclusions and prospects for the future
In conclusion, probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics show significant promise in addressing antibiotic-resistant gut dysbiosis and restoring microbial balance, particularly in cases of Clostridioides difficile-induced diarrhoea. Probiotics have demonstrated their ability to reduce inflam-mation and lower the risk of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, while prebiotics promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria. Synbiotics, combining the benefits of both, offer a synergistic approach to improving gut health. Although treatments like FMT and MRT exist, they remain costly and less accessible. Probiotics face challenges with premature degradation in the upper GI tract, and their use may be limited in certain patient populations. Prebiotics, on the other hand, are widely available and easily integrated into the diet, though further clinical trials are required to fully validate their benefits. Overall, these approaches provide a promising alternative for restoring gut health and

ABSTRACTClostridioides difficile previously known as Clostridium difficile is one of the three most potent human pathogens associated with antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and damage to the colon. Although advanced healthcare facilities with the development of new antibiotics are now available, these are associated with either treatment failure or disease recurrence. Any reason that disturbs the microbiome such as antibiotic treatment, unbalanced diet, stress and chronic disease may allow C. difficile, to adhere, colonize, grow and reproduce and eventually cause disease recurrence. With increasing knowledge about the natural defence mechanism of microbiome against gut path-ogens, interest in non-antibiotic alternatives like prebiotics, synbiotics, probiotics, and postbiotics is quickly evolving. The gut microenvironment can be suitably modified by using prebiotics and probiotics either alone or by using their mixture as synbiotics. The gut microbiome prevents pathogen adhesion either by physical competition or by the proliferation of anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial products. Besides, there are other possible methods such as faecal matter transplantation (FMT) and microbiome replacement therapies (MRT) for the repopulation of the gastrointestinal tract. In this article, we review current treatment strategies for C. difficile infection (CDI) using prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, postbiotic FMT, and MRT. The article will give useful insight into the current therapies of CDI and their future developments.
1.Introduction
Clostridioides difficile is an anaerobic and gram-positive bacterium which linked with array of diseases like diarrhoea to fulminant colitis [1]. C. difficile infection (CDI) reduces the biodiversity of the gut biome and causes intestinal dysbiosis. CDI is a major health issue across the globe associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare-associated infection (HAI). C. difficile primarily elicit the disease by the production of two types of toxins such as TcdA and TcdB that upon endocytosis into the colon, inactivate host GTPases, and disrupt the cytoskeleton and neutrophilic influx, which eventually causes cell apoptosis and necrosis [2]. The rigorous healthcare facilities and appropriate antibiotic treatment are the best treatment options for CDI [3,4]. Despite antibiotics being the preliminary treatment strategies for CDI, they are associated with several side effects. Antibiotics like vancomycin or fidaxomicin are significantly used for the treatment of CDI, however, several case relapses have been found after treatment [5,
6]. The indigenous gut microbiome provides resistance against C. difficile colonization; but antibiotic treatment disrupts the micro-biome and increases susceptibility to CDI [7,8]. The symbiotic in-teractions between resident microbes and the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) play a very significant role in gut homeostasis. However, antibiotic abuse, nutritional choices, and other variables are thought to contribute to gut dysbiosis. Therefore, it is prudent to identify alternatives (non--antibiotics) for the treatment of CDI. In a recent study by V´azquez-Cuesta et al., the researchers aimed to investigate the role of the microbiome as a predictive biomarker for CDI. A total of 753 samples from 657 patients were analyzed, including 247 from patients with CDI, 43 from patients colonized with C. difficile, 63 from healthy individuals, 324 from patients without CDI (NOCDI), and 76 from patients with recurrent CDI (R-CDI). The study revealed significant differences in both alpha and beta diversity, as well as in taxonomic abundance across these groups. Prebiotics are particularly utilized by the host for their health- giving, while probiotics comprise live bacterium that can be beneficial for their health when given in correct doses. Whereas synbiotics are a mixture of probiotics and prebiotics which are good for human health. Through microbial population shifts in the gut, synbiotics start making short-chain fatty acids, which can promote defence against infections, reduce inflammation, increase satiety, and improve bowel function [10,11]. In this article, different strategies of protection against CDI used in present scenarios such as prebiotics, synbiotics, probiotics, FMT, and MBT and their prospects will be discussed in detail.
2.Gut microbiome and their role in human health
The gut microbiome plays crucial role to manage the body’s in-flammatory response, metabolic processes, immunological activity, and even neurological functions [12,13]. It produces vitamins, hormones, and neurotransmitters and causes the breakdown of the dietary com-ponents. The gut microbiome can also influence the host’s metabolic pathways such as absorption and metabolism of nutrients, and synthesis of metabolites. The gut of human beings compasses diverse group of microorganisms such as archaea, bacteria, fungi, and viruses are pre-sent. These microorganisms are responsible for maintaining gut health, by regulating digestion, metabolism, and protection against infections (Fig. 1). The composition of the microbiome is influenced by numerous aspects such as diet, age, and health status. Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes are the prevalent bacterial group present in the gut, whereas Actino-bacteria, Verrucomicrobia, and Proteobacteria are also frequent [14,15]. The most common species of microbiota reported in the gut are Bifidobacterium spp., Bacteroides spp., Clostridium spp., Enterobacter spp., 
Enterococcus spp., Gemella spp., Megasphaera spp., Porphyromonas spp., Pseudomonas spp., Prevotella spp., Rothia spp., Ruminococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Veillonella spp [16]. These microorganisms are usu-ally commensal or mutualists and they primarily aid in regulating metabolism, such as glucose fermentation which produces butyrate, as a bioproduct that works as an essential form of energy for colonocytes. Intestinal microbes also beneficially influence lipid metabolism. They improve protein metabolism by using microbial proteinases and pepti-dases. They are also necessary to produce different vitamins such as vitamin B12, vitamin K, biotin, conjugated linoleic acids etc. They are involved in the degradation of different polyphenols and convert bile acids [17].Many bacteria that are associated with the daily aspects of life can be found in the digestive tract of a healthy individual [18]. The ecology and function of gut bacteria are dynamic in infancy, but they stabilize throughout childhood [19]. These acquired new gut microbiota influ-ence the digestion and the immunologic responses of the host [20,21]. The gut microbiota changes gradually with age in response to devel-oping immune systems [22]. Different environmental factors can also disturb the gut microbiota and are a key indicator of long-term health. The intestinal microbiome not only affects the gut rather it influences every organ of the body via a variety of mechanisms [23]. The external variables can modify the intestinal biome, which offers novel treatment options for some ailments [24]. A healthy gut is necessary for energy harvesting and proper body functions. Besides gut microbiome also af-fects metabolic health, such as blood glucose level, blood pressure, and atherosclerosis, neurological problems, behavioural and inflammatory responses [25]. Recently, the gut microbiome has been considered for its promising characteristic in epilepsy [26].

Supplementing with probiotics e.g., Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium may assist to maintain the balance of microbes in the gut and decrease the chances of the recurrence of CDIs [52,53]. Probiotics can also boost immunity, and thereby guide the body to block the pathogens. Pro-biotics reduce oxidative stress associated with inflammatory diseases.Several findings support probiotics inhibiting pathogen growth and toxicity (Table 1). The use of probiotics to stop the growth of C. difficile has been assessed using various techniques [54,55]. Several studies show that a few species of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can reduce C. difficile’s adherence to the epithelial cell line and mucus of the in-testine [56,57]. Although there is little evidence on the potential effectiveness of probiotics in CDI treatment, most clinical investigations to date have concentrated on prevention. There are some cases where probiotic combination together with any antibiotic prescriptions under C. difficile outbreak, decreased the number of C. difficile cases [58] (Table 1). According to meta-analysis studies, probiotics have continu-ously demonstrated a positive function, in preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD) in children [59,60]. Recently, Lukasik et al. found a multispecies probiotic’s effectiveness in prevent-ing AAD in children [61]. Therefore, using appropriate probiotic composition in children receiving antibiotic treatment could be a pos-sibility to reduce diarrhoea.Meta-analysis has revealed the prospective of two bacterium L. rhamnosus. and S. boulardii in the CDI treatment. Bifidobacteria su-pernatants isolated from the gut of physically fit infants inhibited the growth and adhesion of C. difficile to enterocytes [62]. Whereas the consumption of B. bifidum modulated the gut environment in healthy adults [63]. The mixture of different Lactobacillus species has been found effective in many clinical trials. A probiotic capsule containing four-strain of Lactobacillus improved diarrhoea in CDI patients [64]. The intake of L. acidophilus, L. casei, and L. rhamnosus combination dimin-ished the CDI up to 2.3 cases per ten thousand patients [65]. Similarly, the CDI incidence among immunocompromised patients has been reduced from 1.21 % to 0.11 % using L. plantarum [66]. Adjunct pro-biotics containing L. bulgaricus, L. casei, and S. thermophiles prevented the CDI risk by up to 17 % in patients receiving antibiotic treatment 
[67]. These clinical trial findings emphasize the role of Lactobacillus species as a nontoxic and effective probiotic in CDI prevention and their recurrence. S. boulardii can also significantly help in restoring the antibiotic-disrupted microbiome [68]. S. boulardii CNCM I-745 pro-hibited the consequences and recurrence of CDIs in the hamster model [69–71] (Table 1).Besides the above species, some species of Bacteroides and Clostridium are also used as prebiotic agents for the CDI treatment. B. fragilis strain ZY-312 increased the beneficial microbe of the gut Akkermansia muci-niphila, which prevents C. difficile colonization in the gut [72]. Similarly, B. thetaiotaomicron increased the population of useful bacteria Bacter-oidetes, Proteobacteria and Verruco microbiota and suppressed the C. difficile in the gut [73]. Nonetheless, more clinical trials are essential to confirm the effectiveness of Bacteroides as some of their genera have been found invading the gut microbiome [72,73]. The probiotic mixture containing Bacillus mesentericus, C. butyricum, and S. faecalis, prevented CDIs in elderly patients undergoing femoral fracture surgery (Nagamine, Matsumoto et al., 2019). However, there is no therapeutic usefulness of C. butyricum in adjuvant therapy. In recent times, the probiotic combi-nation containing S. boulardii, or C. butyricum and Lactobacillus species has been widely used for CDI prophylaxis (Nagamine, Matsumoto et al., 2019).Sometimes antibiotics have toxic effects on probiotics while sup-plementation. An appealing solution to the antibiotics’ lethal activity on probiotics may be the physical encapsulation of the latter in a protective shell (Fig. 3). Currently, various polymeric particles have been devel-oped to promote the colonization and presence of probiotics in the GIT, but an efficient, safe, and quick coating with broad-spectrum antibiotic resistance is yet to be developed [74]. The use of natural polyphenols to create a nano armour coating for bacteria in the GIT is a novel approach to protect bacteria from antibiotics [74]. This coating could act as a barrier, allowing bacteria to survive the presence of antibiotics in the GIT. Natural polyphenols, such as those derived from fruits, vegetables, and nuts, have antimicrobial properties that may help to protect bacteria from antibiotics. Additionally, the polyphenol coating could help to reduce the number of antibiotics that are taken up by the bacteria, thus

This coating could also potentially improve the effectiveness of antibiotics by reducing the doses of antibiotics required to achieve the desired therapeutic effect.Pan et al. (2022) recently demonstrated that bacterial cells can be coated in tannic acids and ferric ions ("probiotic nano armour") con-taining a biocompatible coat, without compromising the cells’ activity. This nano armour provides enhanced protection to the probiotic cells in hostile environments, such as high temperatures and acidic conditions, 
and allows them to remain viable and active in the gut. Moreover, the probiotic cells with the nano armour were found to be more effective than uncoated cells in providing protection against pathogens and improving host health [74].

gastrointestinal microbiome, engineered probiotics could be used to retain the balance [75]. These probiotics are specifically designed to target C. difficile and reduce its presence in the intestines [76]. They can also promote the re-establishment of good bacteria like Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus species in the gut, which can further improve digestive health and decrease the risk of infection. Besides restoring the gut microbiome balance, engineered probiotics can also help to lessen the inflammatory reaction and improve the overall health of the digestive system [77].Advancements in gene editing technology have opened new oppor-tunities for probiotic application in CDI treatment. Researchers have been able to use gene editing techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 to modify the genes of certain probiotic strains to improve their efficacy and safety [78]. CRISPR/Cas9 technique can modify the genes of certain probiotic strains to increase their resistance to antibiotics and other drugs, improve their digestive health benefits, and enhance their ability to produce beneficial substances [79]. Additionally, gene editing tech-niques have been used to add new genes to probiotic strains, allowing them to produce compounds with therapeutic benefits, such as anti-inflammatory or anti-cancer agents. Finally, gene editing tech-niques have been used to delete genes from probiotic strains, allowing them to produce fewer harmful substances. Overall, gene editing tech-nology provides a powerful tool to engineer probiotic strains that are more effective and safer for human consumption. By now, several modified probiotics have progressed to the clinical trial stage. The latest advancement in the field of gene editing is CRISPR-Cas9 technology. This technology enables precise editing of any gene sequence by combining DNA-cutting enzymes and RNA-guided proteins. By altering gene sequences, researchers can develop new probiotics with desirable traits [80].Another advancement in the field is the development of gene-editing tools that target specific cells within the probiotic [81]. These tools are used to modify the genetic makeup of the probiotic, which improves the performance of the probiotic or to create new strains with improved stability in the GIT, and increased tolerance to antibiotics. Additionally, gene-editing tools have been used to engineer probiotic bacteria with the ability to produce therapeutic proteins that can help reduce inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity, and fight off infections [78].Gene editing technology is advancing rapidly and is likely to revo-lutionize the world of probiotics. This technology has the potential to revolutionize the way people can improve their health, with potential applications ranging from targeted treatments for diseases to improving the performance of probiotic supplements. With gene editing, scientists can modify the genetic code of microorganisms, allowing for the crea-tion of new probiotic strains with tailored benefits to individual needs. The possibilities for gene editing in the field of probiotics are virtually limitless and could ultimately result in improved health outcomes for people around the world. For example, gene editing could be used to engineer probiotics that are better able to survive in the gut, thereby boosting their effectiveness. It could also be used to create probiotics that are designed to target specific diseases or conditions, allowing for a more personalized approach to health [82]. Additionally, gene editing techniques could allow the development of probiotics that are person-alized to individual dietary requirements, having greater precision and effectiveness. As technology continues to evolve, it is believable to have substantial impact on probiotics research, revolutionizing how they are used for health benefits. Engineered microbes with inflammatory bowel disease applications have also been developed by scientists [83].
5.3.Prebiotic approaches
Earlier the prebiotics definition was limited to the non-digestible food item which significantly benefited the host but later, it was broadened to encompass both carbohydrates (e.g., Fructo- oligosaccharides (FOS), inulin, lactulose, galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS)) and dietary prebiotics. Dietary prebiotics are described as “the 
ingredients that positively affect the composition and/or activity of the gut microbiome for the health profit of the host” [84]. However, the most important aspect of prebiotics is their association with human well-being, as their beneficial effects are further enhanced through cross-feeding [85].Prebiotics can help to renew the overall healthy balance of microbes in the gut as well as reduce the risk of recurrence of C. difficile infections [86]. They must meet criteria such as resistance to acidic pH, non-hydrolysable by host enzymes, non-absorbable in the GIT, and fermentable by intestinal microorganisms [87]. For carbohydrate-derived prebiotics the degree of polymerization must be ≥3 [88].There are several types of prebiotics such as glucose-derived oligo-saccharides, galacto-oligosaccharides, pectic oligosaccharides, fructans, starch, and other oligosaccharides carbohydrates (OSCs) which are very useful in mitigating CDIs (Table 2). Naturally different dietary food products like pulses and vegetables are rich sources of prebiotics but recently, prebiotics have been obtained from seaweed and microalgae as well [89]. However, due to its lower concentration in foods, nowadays industries are producing it at large scales.Over the past few years there has been an increased role of poly-phenols as prebiotic agents. encompasses the transfer of faecal matter from a physically fit person’s stool to a recipient that helps to repair the gut microbiome and treat conditions like inflammatory bowel and antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (Fig. 4). FMT is the utmost effective form of MRT for recurrent CDI cases, with a recovery rate of over 90 %. FMT has been used for over 1700 years in traditional systems of medicine to treat a variety of illnesses [110]. Recent research has revealed that healthy commensal bacteria in the gut can collaborate to produce beneficial metabolites with anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and even antifungal properties. These metabolites might be accountable for the health-promoting effects of FMT. In addition, FMT also modulates the immune response, reduces inflammation, and restores a balanced gut microbiota. Kamierczak-Siedlecka et al. studied the molecular mechanisms of FMT and found that several bacterial species are important for the successful outcome of FMT, including Bacteroides fragilis, Roseburia intestinalis, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii [111].FMT is a rapidly developing therapeutic approach that has become a focus of biomedical and clinical studies. It is used as a last resort when other therapies for C. difficile have failed. FMT is specifically composed of well-known probiotic microbes that have been selected for their ability to provide health benefits through one or more mechanisms. In clinical studies, fecal matter transfer is generally safe and effective in treating CDI with a success rate of over 90 % and few adverse effects reported [112]. As research continues, the potential benefits of faecal matter transfer may become clearer. However, further clinical trials are essential to establish the efficacy of FMT in CDI [111].Before samples can be accepted, donors must be meticulously tested and vetted. To preserve the bacteria, the stool samples are diluted in saline and filtered, and then glycerol is added. This sample is then stored at 80 
◦C. The sample is administered in liquid form to the transplant recipient. It can be transported either through the anus into the large intestine using a colonoscopy, or via the nose and into the small intestine using a nasoduodenal tube (NGT). Additionally, the donor’s stool sam-ple is tested for any dangerous bacteria, viruses, and parasites. FMT helps to restore a healthy bacterial balance in the colon. FMT is usually performed with a colonoscopy, however, it can also be performed with a less common approach, such as an NGT. During a colonoscopy, the co-lonoscope is inserted into the colon and moved through the total length of the colon. As the colonoscope is removed, the stool is delivered into the colon. The stool contains healthy bacteria and other microbial or-ganisms that help to restore a healthy bacterial balance in the colon. Additionally, FMT can help to reduce symptoms related to the bowels, Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis, and CDI.Faecal transplantation via colonoscopy was found very suitable in the treatment of recurrent CDI, which can recur in up to 50 % of patients receiving antibiotics [113]. The potential role of FMT to treat CDI has created a new area of research into microbiome-based restorative therapies.A pooled analysis of recurrent CDI cases by FMT via colonoscopy or nasogastric tube (NGT) has been conducted by Postigo and Kim, to determine the efficacy of the procedure. The results indicated that FMT by colonoscopy or NGT could be an effective solution for the recurrent CDI, regardless of procedure alterations. However, further studies are required to explore the optimal delivery route for FMT [114,115].The latest report of the treatment of a 78-year-old man suffering from Pseudomembranous Colitis due to C. difficile persistence in the stool sample from New Delhi, India. FMT by a healthy person’s stool helped to cure these severe cases (Link20.01.22).There are some unsuccessful cases of FMT as well. For example, In Italy while treating CDI with FMT (colonoscopy) only 69 % of patients recovered by a single faecal dose, whereas the remaining 31 % required repeat infusions [116]. The recovery rate of patients suffering from CDI varied from 14 % to 59 % in the United States due to application of non-specific antibiotics, severe and fulminant CDI, and pseudomem-branous colitis. Moreover, FMT was associated with numerous side ef-fects such as abdominal cramping, bloating, diarrhoea, and nausea 
[117]. Besides two patients receiving FMT from the same donor suffered from bacteriemia caused by E. coli, and one patient died [118]. Thus, the selection of suitable donors and recipients is very crucial for performing FMT.
5.7.Treatment of C. difficile by targeting toxins A (TcdA) and B (TcdB)
There are various antibiotics such as metronidazole or vancomycin available for CDI treatment. These antibiotics mainly inhibit the toxins (TcdA and TcdB) secreted by C. difficile, thus preventing further colon damage. Additionally, probiotics may be utilized to reinstate the balance of microbes in the gut. Treatment of C. difficile typically involves the use of antibiotics to decrease the bacterial counts. However, in some cases, antibiotics may not be enough to eradicate the infection. In these cases, targeting the toxins produced by C. difficile may reduce the severity of the infection. TcdA and TcdB are two of the most potent toxins produced by C. difficile. To target these toxins, several medications have been developed. These medications can include antibody-based therapies or small molecule inhibitors that prevent toxin production or neutralize its activity. In some cases, a combination of antibiotics and other treat-ments may be necessary to successfully treat C. difficile.Scientists have recently proposed that serine proteases from two probiotic strains, Saccharomyces boulardii and Bacillus clausii, could be used to prevent CDI. A serine protease from S. boulardii has been shown to disrupt the quorum sensing mechanism of C. difficile, an important regulatory mechanism. Moreover, this protease was also shown to effectively suppress the toxin TcdA. Similarly, a protease from B. clausii was found to be effective against TcdB. Both proteases have demon-strated efficacy in vivo and in vitro, suggesting that they may be prom-ising targets for further research regarding the prevention of CDI [119]. The toxins TcdA and TcdB required for C. difficile-caused diarrhoea are produced by pathogenic strains. An alternate treatment fare CDI that has revealed encouraging outcomes in preclinical and clinical investigations is the administration of anti-toxin antibodies [120].In a recent study, Hunag and McCreary reported that Clostridium butyricum is useful in treating a variety of gastrointestinal conditions. C. difficile was reported to be significantly inhibited by supernatants of the C. butyricum MIYAIRI 588 strain (CBM588). A proteinaceous component may be important in preventing C. difficile growth in vitro, according to features of the supernatant from CBM 588 that are heat- and pH-labile [121]. It has been established that recombinant CBM 588 bacteriocin (CBM-B) has an inhibitory effect against C. difficile, however, spore germination and outgrowth were unaffected. By lowering the expression of a toxin regulator when used at sub-lethal concentrations, CBM-B could partially suppress the expression of toxins (tcdA and tcdB). A mice infected with CDI, intra-rectal injection of CBM-B in combination with vancomycin lead to in less body weight loss and a lower C. difficile bacterial count in faeces than did CBM-B or vancomycin administration alone. As a result, CBM-B from CBM 588 has the potential to be an in-hibitor of C. difficile and a possible therapeutic therapy for CDI.The effectiveness of human monoclonal antibodies (HuMab) and polyclonal antibodies against C. difficile toxins TcdA and TcdB were examined in a genotobiotic piglet model of CDI by Steele et al. [122,123] The results showed that TcdB was a major virulence factor contributing to both systemic and gastrointestinal (GI) tract diseases. Administration of anti-TcdB antibodies alone or in combination with anti-TcdA completely prevented systemic CDI in piglets and significantly reduced GI lesions. In contrast, pigs who received only anti-TcdA experienced severe GI and systemic illnesses with a 67–83 % death rate, performing worse than the control animals which had been given a placebo [123].
5.8.Postbiotic approach against CDI
The concept of postbiotics, which emerged in 2021, is currently being widely studied [124]. Postbiotics are a form of metabolic 
C. Singh et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Medicine in Microecology 24 (2025) 100121 9 

byproducts or non-viable bacterial products produced by probiotic mi-croorganisms, which exert a biological effect on the host. Postbiotics are composed of functional bioactive compounds created in an anaerobic matrix, resulting from the fermentation of prebiotics and other organic nutrients which generate energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate. These byproducts, often of low molecular weight, include short-chain fatty acids, microbial cell fragments, extracellular polysaccharides, cell lysates, teichoic acid, vitamins, and more [125]. While prebiotics and probiotics are currently the most popular products on the market, postbiotics are gaining an increasing amount of attention due to their numerous health benefits (Fig. 5). Probiotics are increasingly recognized as a valuable tool for restoring balance to the intestinal microbiota disrupted by factors such as antibiotic therapy. This disruption can create an environment conducive to the overgrowth of C. difficile, leading to a rise in C. difficile-associated infections. Although many probiotics have demonstrated in vitro efficacy in inhibiting the growth or toxicity of C. difficile, their use in treating or preventing CDI remains limited due to a lack of robust clinical evidence. Only a few strains, notably Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii, have been extensively studied. The growing understanding of how probiotics combat C. difficile through various mechanisms reviewed here suggests that these live biotherapeutic agents hold promise for CDI management. However, there is a need for more rigorous and standardized clinical studies to evaluate probiotic products in conjunction with antibiotics, to identify the most effective candidates for preventing or treating C. difficile infections [55]. Given these insights, it is likely that the de-mand for postbiotic supplements will rise in the future. Postbiotics, known for their antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodu-latory properties, are emerging as a promising option for treating or preventing CDI. Research has demonstrated that postbiotics can inhibit the growth of Clostridium difficile in both in vitro studies and animal models, as well as reduce toxin production. Furthermore, postbiotic therapy appears beneficial for premature infants, who frequently lack beneficial bacteria. This therapy has been shown to mitigate inflam-mation, improve digestion, and enhance overall health in these vulnerable patients [121,126].Postbiotics can be administered via food, supplements, or enemas. These beneficial compounds are believed to offer a range of protective effects, such as producing substances that reduce inflammation, bolster the body’s natural defenses, and support healthy intestinal tissue. Evi-dence suggests that postbiotic therapy is both safe and effective in managing various intestinal disorders in premature infants [127].
In a recent study, Luenglusontigit et al. first used a high-throughput screening approach to isolate and identify E. faecalis strains that pro-duced bacteriocin-like compounds [128]. Screening of bacteriocin pro-duction of E. faecalis PK1201 was achieved through proteolytic enzyme treatment, followed by whole genome sequencing to characterize bacteriocin-encoding genes. A postbiotic of E. faecalis PK1201 was then prepared using neutralized cell-free supernatant or bacterial cell lysate, which was screened for antimicrobial activity using agar well diffusion. The lyophilized cell-free supernatant (LCFS) was subsequently tested for its minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against C. difficile 630. Morphological changes of C. difficile were observed under scanning electron microscopes. The LCFS at both sub-MIC and MIC concentrations were used to evaluate anti-spore germination activity. Finally, the safety of the postbiotic was evaluated using the Galleria mellonella model. The efficacy and safety of LCFS has illuminated the role of postbiotics in pharmaceutical products for the control of CDI [128].Postbiotics have demonstrated the ability to support gut microbiota health and reduce inflammation, which may help lower the risk of CDI. They may also be effective in treating recurrent CDI by restoring gut microbiota balance. In addition, postbiotics show great promise as an adjunctive treatment for CDI due to their capacity to inhibit bacterial growth, disrupt biofilms, and reduce toxin production, offering a po-tential solution to antibiotic-resistant pathogens [129]. However, further research is needed to confirm the efficacy and safety of these compounds in treating CDI.
6.Conclusions and prospects for the future
In conclusion, probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics show significant promise in addressing antibiotic-resistant gut dysbiosis and restoring microbial balance, particularly in cases of Clostridioides difficile-induced diarrhoea. Probiotics have demonstrated their ability to reduce inflam-mation and lower the risk of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, while prebiotics promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria. Synbiotics, combining the benefits of both, offer a synergistic approach to improving gut health. Although treatments like FMT and MRT exist, they remain costly and less accessible. Probiotics face challenges with premature degradation in the upper GI tract, and their use may be limited in certain patient populations. Prebiotics, on the other hand, are widely available and easily integrated into the diet, though further clinical trials are required to fully validate their benefits. Overall, these approaches provide a promising alternative for restoring gut health and

Potential therapeutic solution for Clostridioides difficile infection: Current scenario and future prospectsChandrashekhar Singha, Anjali Singhb, Deepjyoti Singhc, Richa Upadhyayd,*aMaharishi School of Science and Humanities, Maharishi University of Information Technology, Lucknow, 226013, Uttar Pradesh, IndiabLaboratory of Cell Cycles of Algae, Centre Algatech, Institute of Microbiology of Czech Academy of Sciences, Novaradaska, 23737981, Trebon, Czech RepubliccDepartment of Entomology and Plant Pathology, North Carolina State University, USAdDepartment of Botany, Mihir Bhoj PG College, Dadri, GB Nagar, 203207, Uttar Pradesh, IndiaARTICLE INFOKeywords:Gut microbiotaPolyphenolsFecal microbiota transplantAntibioticsC. difficile
ABSTRACTClostridioides difficile previously known as Clostridium difficile is one of the three most potent human pathogens associated with antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and damage to the colon. Although advanced healthcare facilities with the development of new antibiotics are now available, these are associated with either treatment failure or disease recurrence. Any reason that disturbs the microbiome such as antibiotic treatment, unbalanced diet, stress and chronic disease may allow C. difficile, to adhere, colonize, grow and reproduce and eventually cause disease recurrence. With increasing knowledge about the natural defence mechanism of microbiome against gut path-ogens, interest in non-antibiotic alternatives like prebiotics, synbiotics, probiotics, and postbiotics is quickly evolving. The gut microenvironment can be suitably modified by using prebiotics and probiotics either alone or by using their mixture as synbiotics. The gut microbiome prevents pathogen adhesion either by physical competition or by the proliferation of anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial products. Besides, there are other possible methods such as faecal matter transplantation (FMT) and microbiome replacement therapies (MRT) for the repopulation of the gastrointestinal tract. In this article, we review current treatment strategies for C. difficile infection (CDI) using prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, postbiotic FMT, and MRT. The article will give useful insight into the current therapies of CDI and their future developments.
1.Introduction
Clostridioides difficile is an anaerobic and gram-positive bacterium which linked with array of diseases like diarrhoea to fulminant colitis [1]. C. difficile infection (CDI) reduces the biodiversity of the gut biome and causes intestinal dysbiosis. CDI is a major health issue across the globe associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare-associated infection (HAI). C. difficile primarily elicit the disease by the production of two types of toxins such as TcdA and TcdB that upon endocytosis into the colon, inactivate host GTPases, and disrupt the cytoskeleton and neutrophilic influx, which eventually causes cell apoptosis and necrosis [2]. The rigorous healthcare facilities and appropriate antibiotic treatment are the best treatment options for CDI [3,4]. Despite antibiotics being the preliminary treatment strategies for CDI, they are associated with several side effects. Antibiotics like vancomycin or fidaxomicin are significantly used for the treatment of CDI, however, several case relapses have been found after treatment [5,
6]. The indigenous gut microbiome provides resistance against C. difficile colonization; but antibiotic treatment disrupts the micro-biome and increases susceptibility to CDI [7,8]. The symbiotic in-teractions between resident microbes and the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) play a very significant role in gut homeostasis. However, antibiotic abuse, nutritional choices, and other variables are thought to contribute to gut dysbiosis. Therefore, it is prudent to identify alternatives (non--antibiotics) for the treatment of CDI. In a recent study by V´azquez-Cuesta et al., the researchers aimed to investigate the role of the microbiome as a predictive biomarker for CDI. A total of 753 samples from 657 patients were analyzed, including 247 from patients with CDI, 43 from patients colonized with C. difficile, 63 from healthy individuals, 324 from patients without CDI (NOCDI), and 76 from patients with recurrent CDI (R-CDI). The study revealed significant differences in both alpha and beta diversity, as well as in taxonomic abundance across these groups. Several genera were identified as key biomarkers for CDI (Bac-teroides, Proteus, Paraprevotella, Robinsoniella), R-CDI (Veillonella,

Prebiotics are particularly utilized by the host for their health- giving, while probiotics comprise live bacterium that can be beneficial for their health when given in correct doses. Whereas synbiotics are a mixture of probiotics and prebiotics which are good for human health. Through microbial population shifts in the gut, synbiotics start making short-chain fatty acids, which can promote defence against infections, reduce inflammation, increase satiety, and improve bowel function [10,11]. In this article, different strategies of protection against CDI used in present scenarios such as prebiotics, synbiotics, probiotics, FMT, and MBT and their prospects will be discussed in detail.
2.Gut microbiome and their role in human health
The gut microbiome plays crucial role to manage the body’s in-flammatory response, metabolic processes, immunological activity, and even neurological functions [12,13]. It produces vitamins, hormones, and neurotransmitters and causes the breakdown of the dietary com-ponents. The gut microbiome can also influence the host’s metabolic pathways such as absorption and metabolism of nutrients, and synthesis of metabolites. The gut of human beings compasses diverse group of microorganisms such as archaea, bacteria, fungi, and viruses are pre-sent. These microorganisms are responsible for maintaining gut health, by regulating digestion, metabolism, and protection against infections (Fig. 1). The composition of the microbiome is influenced by numerous aspects such as diet, age, and health status. Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes are the prevalent bacterial group present in the gut, whereas Actino-bacteria, Verrucomicrobia, and Proteobacteria are also frequent [14,15]. The most common species of microbiota reported in the gut are Bifidobacterium spp., Bacteroides spp., Clostridium spp., Enterobacter spp., 
Enterococcus spp., Gemella spp., Megasphaera spp., Porphyromonas spp., Pseudomonas spp., Prevotella spp., Rothia spp., Ruminococcus spp., Streptococcus spp., Veillonella spp [16]. These microorganisms are usu-ally commensal or mutualists and they primarily aid in regulating metabolism, such as glucose fermentation which produces butyrate, as a bioproduct that works as an essential form of energy for colonocytes. Intestinal microbes also beneficially influence lipid metabolism. They improve protein metabolism by using microbial proteinases and pepti-dases. They are also necessary to produce different vitamins such as vitamin B12, vitamin K, biotin, conjugated linoleic acids etc. They are involved in the degradation of different polyphenols and convert bile acids [17].Many bacteria that are associated with the daily aspects of life can be found in the digestive tract of a healthy individual [18]. The ecology and function of gut bacteria are dynamic in infancy, but they stabilize throughout childhood [19]. These acquired new gut microbiota influ-ence the digestion and the immunologic responses of the host [20,21]. The gut microbiota changes gradually with age in response to devel-oping immune systems [22]. Different environmental factors can also disturb the gut microbiota and are a key indicator of long-term health. The intestinal microbiome not only affects the gut rather it influences every organ of the body via a variety of mechanisms [23]. The external variables can modify the intestinal biome, which offers novel treatment options for some ailments [24]. A healthy gut is necessary for energy harvesting and proper body functions. Besides gut microbiome also af-fects metabolic health, such as blood glucose level, blood pressure, and atherosclerosis, neurological problems, behavioural and inflammatory responses [25]. Recently, the gut microbiome has been considered for its promising characteristic in epilepsy [26].

Supplementing with probiotics e.g., Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium may assist to maintain the balance of microbes in the gut and decrease the chances of the recurrence of CDIs [52,53]. Probiotics can also boost immunity, and thereby guide the body to block the pathogens. Pro-biotics reduce oxidative stress associated with inflammatory diseases.Several findings support probiotics inhibiting pathogen growth and toxicity (Table 1). The use of probiotics to stop the growth of C. difficile has been assessed using various techniques [54,55]. Several studies show that a few species of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can reduce C. difficile’s adherence to the epithelial cell line and mucus of the in-testine [56,57]. Although there is little evidence on the potential effectiveness of probiotics in CDI treatment, most clinical investigations to date have concentrated on prevention. There are some cases where probiotic combination together with any antibiotic prescriptions under C. difficile outbreak, decreased the number of C. difficile cases [58] (Table 1). According to meta-analysis studies, probiotics have continu-ously demonstrated a positive function, in preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD) in children [59,60]. Recently, Lukasik et al. found a multispecies probiotic’s effectiveness in prevent-ing AAD in children [61]. Therefore, using appropriate probiotic composition in children receiving antibiotic treatment could be a pos-sibility to reduce diarrhoea.Meta-analysis has revealed the prospective of two bacterium L. rhamnosus. and S. boulardii in the CDI treatment. Bifidobacteria su-pernatants isolated from the gut of physically fit infants inhibited the growth and adhesion of C. difficile to enterocytes [62]. Whereas the consumption of B. bifidum modulated the gut environment in healthy adults [63]. The mixture of different Lactobacillus species has been found effective in many clinical trials. A probiotic capsule containing four-strain of Lactobacillus improved diarrhoea in CDI patients [64]. The intake of L. acidophilus, L. casei, and L. rhamnosus combination dimin-ished the CDI up to 2.3 cases per ten thousand patients [65]. Similarly, the CDI incidence among immunocompromised patients has been reduced from 1.21 % to 0.11 % using L. plantarum [66]. Adjunct pro-biotics containing L. bulgaricus, L. casei, and S. thermophiles prevented the CDI risk by up to 17 % in patients receiving antibiotic treatment 
[67]. These clinical trial findings emphasize the role of Lactobacillus species as a nontoxic and effective probiotic in CDI prevention and their recurrence. S. boulardii can also significantly help in restoring the antibiotic-disrupted microbiome [68]. S. boulardii CNCM I-745 pro-hibited the consequences and recurrence of CDIs in the hamster model [69–71] (Table 1).Besides the above species, some species of Bacteroides and Clostridium are also used as prebiotic agents for the CDI treatment. B. fragilis strain ZY-312 increased the beneficial microbe of the gut Akkermansia muci-niphila, which prevents C. difficile colonization in the gut [72]. Similarly, B. thetaiotaomicron increased the population of useful bacteria Bacter-oidetes, Proteobacteria and Verruco microbiota and suppressed the C. difficile in the gut [73]. Nonetheless, more clinical trials are essential to confirm the effectiveness of Bacteroides as some of their genera have been found invading the gut microbiome [72,73]. The probiotic mixture containing Bacillus mesentericus, C. butyricum, and S. faecalis, prevented CDIs in elderly patients undergoing femoral fracture surgery (Nagamine, Matsumoto et al., 2019). However, there is no therapeutic usefulness of C. butyricum in adjuvant therapy. In recent times, the probiotic combi-nation containing S. boulardii, or C. butyricum and Lactobacillus species has been widely used for CDI prophylaxis (Nagamine, Matsumoto et al., 2019).Sometimes antibiotics have toxic effects on probiotics while sup-plementation. An appealing solution to the antibiotics’ lethal activity on probiotics may be the physical encapsulation of the latter in a protective shell (Fig. 3). Currently, various polymeric particles have been devel-oped to promote the colonization and presence of probiotics in the GIT, but an efficient, safe, and quick coating with broad-spectrum antibiotic resistance is yet to be developed [74]. The use of natural polyphenols to create a nano armour coating for bacteria in the GIT is a novel approach to protect bacteria from antibiotics [74]. This coating could act as a barrier, allowing bacteria to survive the presence of antibiotics in the GIT. Natural polyphenols, such as those derived from fruits, vegetables, and nuts, have antimicrobial properties that may help to protect bacteria from antibiotics. Additionally, the polyphenol coating could help to reduce the number of antibiotics that are taken up by the bacteria, thus

gastrointestinal microbiome, engineered probiotics could be used to retain the balance [75]. These probiotics are specifically designed to target C. difficile and reduce its presence in the intestines [76]. They can also promote the re-establishment of good bacteria like Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus species in the gut, which can further improve digestive health and decrease the risk of infection. Besides restoring the gut microbiome balance, engineered probiotics can also help to lessen the inflammatory reaction and improve the overall health of the digestive system [77].Advancements in gene editing technology have opened new oppor-tunities for probiotic application in CDI treatment. Researchers have been able to use gene editing techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 to modify the genes of certain probiotic strains to improve their efficacy and safety [78]. CRISPR/Cas9 technique can modify the genes of certain probiotic strains to increase their resistance to antibiotics and other drugs, improve their digestive health benefits, and enhance their ability to produce beneficial substances [79]. Additionally, gene editing tech-niques have been used to add new genes to probiotic strains, allowing them to produce compounds with therapeutic benefits, such as anti-inflammatory or anti-cancer agents. Finally, gene editing tech-niques have been used to delete genes from probiotic strains, allowing them to produce fewer harmful substances. Overall, gene editing tech-nology provides a powerful tool to engineer probiotic strains that are more effective and safer for human consumption. By now, several modified probiotics have progressed to the clinical trial stage. The latest advancement in the field of gene editing is CRISPR-Cas9 technology. This technology enables precise editing of any gene sequence by combining DNA-cutting enzymes and RNA-guided proteins. By altering gene sequences, researchers can develop new probiotics with desirable traits [80].Another advancement in the field is the development of gene-editing tools that target specific cells within the probiotic [81]. These tools are used to modify the genetic makeup of the probiotic, which improves the performance of the probiotic or to create new strains with improved stability in the GIT, and increased tolerance to antibiotics. Additionally, gene-editing tools have been used to engineer probiotic bacteria with the ability to produce therapeutic proteins that can help reduce inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity, and fight off infections [78].Gene editing technology is advancing rapidly and is likely to revo-lutionize the world of probiotics. This technology has the potential to revolutionize the way people can improve their health, with potential applications ranging from targeted treatments for diseases to improving the performance of probiotic supplements. With gene editing, scientists can modify the genetic code of microorganisms, allowing for the crea-tion of new probiotic strains with tailored benefits to individual needs. The possibilities for gene editing in the field of probiotics are virtually limitless and could ultimately result in improved health outcomes for people around the world. For example, gene editing could be used to engineer probiotics that are better able to survive in the gut, thereby boosting their effectiveness. It could also be used to create probiotics that are designed to target specific diseases or conditions, allowing for a more personalized approach to health [82]. Additionally, gene editing techniques could allow the development of probiotics that are person-alized to individual dietary requirements, having greater precision and effectiveness. As technology continues to evolve, it is believable to have substantial impact on probiotics research, revolutionizing how they are used for health benefits. Engineered microbes with inflammatory bowel disease applications have also been developed by scientists [83].
5.3.Prebiotic approaches
Earlier the prebiotics definition was limited to the non-digestible food item which significantly benefited the host but later, it was broadened to encompass both carbohydrates (e.g., Fructo- oligosaccharides (FOS), inulin, lactulose, galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS)) and dietary prebiotics. Dietary prebiotics are described as “the 
ingredients that positively affect the composition and/or activity of the gut microbiome for the health profit of the host” [84]. However, the most important aspect of prebiotics is their association with human well-being, as their beneficial effects are further enhanced through cross-feeding [85].Prebiotics can help to renew the overall healthy balance of microbes in the gut as well as reduce the risk of recurrence of C. difficile infections [86]. They must meet criteria such as resistance to acidic pH, non-hydrolysable by host enzymes, non-absorbable in the GIT, and fermentable by intestinal microorganisms [87]. For carbohydrate-derived prebiotics the degree of polymerization must be ≥3 [88].There are several types of prebiotics such as glucose-derived oligo-saccharides, galacto-oligosaccharides, pectic oligosaccharides, fructans, starch, and other oligosaccharides carbohydrates (OSCs) which are very useful in mitigating CDIs (Table 2). Naturally different dietary food products like pulses and vegetables are rich sources of prebiotics but recently, prebiotics have been obtained from seaweed and microalgae as well [89]. However, due to its lower concentration in foods, nowadays industries are producing it at large scales.Over the past few years there has been an increased role of poly-phenols as prebiotic agents. encompasses the transfer of faecal matter from a physically fit person’s stool to a recipient that helps to repair the gut microbiome and treat conditions like inflammatory bowel and antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (Fig. 4). FMT is the utmost effective form of MRT for recurrent CDI cases, with a recovery rate of over 90 %. FMT has been used for over 1700 years in traditional systems of medicine to treat a variety of illnesses [110]. Recent research has revealed that healthy commensal bacteria in the gut can collaborate to produce beneficial metabolites with anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and even antifungal properties. These metabolites might be accountable for the health-promoting effects of FMT. In addition, FMT also modulates the immune response, reduces inflammation, and restores a balanced gut microbiota. Kamierczak-Siedlecka et al. studied the molecular mechanisms of FMT and found that several bacterial species are important for the successful outcome of FMT, including Bacteroides fragilis, Roseburia intestinalis, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii [111].FMT is a rapidly developing therapeutic approach that has become a focus of biomedical and clinical studies. It is used as a last resort when other therapies for C. difficile have failed. FMT is specifically composed of well-known probiotic microbes that have been selected for their ability to provide health benefits through one or more mechanisms. In clinical studies, fecal matter transfer is generally safe and effective in treating CDI with a success rate of over 90 % and few adverse effects reported [112]. As research continues, the potential benefits of faecal matter transfer may become clearer. However, further clinical trials are essential to establish the efficacy of FMT in CDI [111].Before samples can be accepted, donors must be meticulously tested and vetted. To preserve the bacteria, the stool samples are diluted in saline and filtered, and then glycerol is added. This sample is then stored at 80 
◦C. The sample is administered in liquid form to the transplant recipient. It can be transported either through the anus into the large intestine using a colonoscopy, or via the nose and into the small intestine using a nasoduodenal tube (NGT). Additionally, the donor’s stool sam-ple is tested for any dangerous bacteria, viruses, and parasites. FMT helps to restore a healthy bacterial balance in the colon. FMT is usually performed with a colonoscopy, however, it can also be performed with a less common approach, such as an NGT. During a colonoscopy, the co-lonoscope is inserted into the colon and moved through the total length of the colon. As the colonoscope is removed, the stool is delivered into the colon. The stool contains healthy bacteria and other microbial or-ganisms that help to restore a healthy bacterial balance in the colon. Additionally, FMT can help to reduce symptoms related to the bowels, Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis, and CDI.Faecal transplantation via colonoscopy was found very suitable in the treatment of recurrent CDI, which can recur in up to 50 % of patients receiving antibiotics [113]. The potential role of FMT to treat CDI has created a new area of research into microbiome-based restorative therapies.A pooled analysis of recurrent CDI cases by FMT via colonoscopy or nasogastric tube (NGT) has been conducted by Postigo and Kim, to determine the efficacy of the procedure. The results indicated that FMT by colonoscopy or NGT could be an effective solution for the recurrent CDI, regardless of procedure alterations. However, further studies are required to explore the optimal delivery route for FMT [114,115].The latest report of the treatment of a 78-year-old man suffering from Pseudomembranous Colitis due to C. difficile persistence in the stool sample from New Delhi, India. FMT by a healthy person’s stool helped to cure these severe cases (Link20.01.22).There are some unsuccessful cases of FMT as well. For example, In Italy while treating CDI with FMT (colonoscopy) only 69 % of patients recovered by a single faecal dose, whereas the remaining 31 % required repeat infusions [116]. The recovery rate of patients suffering from CDI varied from 14 % to 59 % in the United States due to application of non-specific antibiotics, severe and fulminant CDI, and pseudomem-branous colitis. Moreover, FMT was associated with numerous side ef-fects such as abdominal cramping, bloating, diarrhoea, and nausea 
[117]. Besides two patients receiving FMT from the same donor suffered from bacteriemia caused by E. coli, and one patient died [118]. Thus, the selection of suitable donors and recipients is very crucial for performing FMT.
5.7.Treatment of C. difficile by targeting toxins A (TcdA) and B (TcdB)
There are various antibiotics such as metronidazole or vancomycin available for CDI treatment. These antibiotics mainly inhibit the toxins (TcdA and TcdB) secreted by C. difficile, thus preventing further colon damage. Additionally, probiotics may be utilized to reinstate the balance of microbes in the gut. Treatment of C. difficile typically involves the use of antibiotics to decrease the bacterial counts. However, in some cases, antibiotics may not be enough to eradicate the infection. In these cases, targeting the toxins produced by C. difficile may reduce the severity of the infection. TcdA and TcdB are two of the most potent toxins produced by C. difficile. To target these toxins, several medications have been developed. These medications can include antibody-based therapies or small molecule inhibitors that prevent toxin production or neutralize its activity. In some cases, a combination of antibiotics and other treat-ments may be necessary to successfully treat C. difficile.Scientists have recently proposed that serine proteases from two probiotic strains, Saccharomyces boulardii and Bacillus clausii, could be used to prevent CDI. A serine protease from S. boulardii has been shown to disrupt the quorum sensing mechanism of C. difficile, an important regulatory mechanism. Moreover, this protease was also shown to effectively suppress the toxin TcdA. Similarly, a protease from B. clausii was found to be effective against TcdB. Both proteases have demon-strated efficacy in vivo and in vitro, suggesting that they may be prom-ising targets for further research regarding the prevention of CDI [119]. The toxins TcdA and TcdB required for C. difficile-caused diarrhoea are produced by pathogenic strains. An alternate treatment fare CDI that has revealed encouraging outcomes in preclinical and clinical investigations is the administration of anti-toxin antibodies [120].In a recent study, Hunag and McCreary reported that Clostridium butyricum is useful in treating a variety of gastrointestinal conditions. C. difficile was reported to be significantly inhibited by supernatants of the C. butyricum MIYAIRI 588 strain (CBM588). A proteinaceous component may be important in preventing C. difficile growth in vitro, according to features of the supernatant from CBM 588 that are heat- and pH-labile [121]. It has been established that recombinant CBM 588 bacteriocin (CBM-B) has an inhibitory effect against C. difficile, however, spore germination and outgrowth were unaffected. By lowering the expression of a toxin regulator when used at sub-lethal concentrations, CBM-B could partially suppress the expression of toxins (tcdA and tcdB). A mice infected with CDI, intra-rectal injection of CBM-B in combination with vancomycin lead to in less body weight loss and a lower C. difficile bacterial count in faeces than did CBM-B or vancomycin administration alone. As a result, CBM-B from CBM 588 has the potential to be an in-hibitor of C. difficile and a possible therapeutic therapy for CDI.The effectiveness of human monoclonal antibodies (HuMab) and polyclonal antibodies against C. difficile toxins TcdA and TcdB were examined in a genotobiotic piglet model of CDI by Steele et al. [122,123] The results showed that TcdB was a major virulence factor contributing to both systemic and gastrointestinal (GI) tract diseases. Administration of anti-TcdB antibodies alone or in combination with anti-TcdA completely prevented systemic CDI in piglets and significantly reduced GI lesions. In contrast, pigs who received only anti-TcdA experienced severe GI and systemic illnesses with a 67–83 % death rate, performing worse than the control animals which had been given a placebo [123].
5.8.Postbiotic approach against CDI
The concept of postbiotics, which emerged in 2021, is currently being widely studied [124]. Postbiotics are a form of metabolic
